articles.title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
articles.content:
The PHP team has patched several vulnerabilities, including a 9.2-rated request-smuggling flaw. The risk depends on server configuration, reinforcing the need to inventory PHP across enterprise environments.

PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

  • The threat actor gets in through the web application.
  • Reads the configuration file;
  • Dumps the customer database;
  • Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

  • Is session upload progress on?
  • Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?
  • Does php-cgi face the internet?
  • Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

articles.title: F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
articles.content:
Just two months after it fixed a critical RCE bug, F5 has released out of band patches for five more critical vulnerabilities in its Access Policy Manager.

F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic.

All five of the patches are stack-based buffer overflows that could let an unauthenticated threat actor terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

F5 described them as follows:

  • CVE-2026-121805: When an iRule that processes client traffic using the PEM:subscriber command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-120292: When an HTTP profile and an iRule using the MR:message route command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-120285: When an HTTP profile and an iRule containing the PSC:ip_address command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-116953: When an iRule that processes client traffic using the GENERICMESSAGE:route command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);
  • CVE-2026-123637: When BIG-IP APM is provisioned and a per-request policy that includes the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE).

The company said there are no mitigations for the flaws and advised customers to install the hotfixes on vulnerable devices, and to upgrade vulnerable versions without a listed fix to a patched version.

In the same batch of out of band patches, F5 also addressed CVE-2026-126822, a high severity integer underflow vulnerability in BIG-IP APM SAML that could also crash TMM and lead to denial of service.

This is the second critical issue in two months for APM; September’s zero-day bug was already being exploited when it was patched. F5 did not indicate that any of the current batch is as yet being exploited but given the growing trend of attacks on edge devices by criminals and nation-state threat actors, admins should update systems as soon as possible.

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

articles.title: Rio de Janeiro introduces biometric birth registration for mothers and newborns
articles.content:
Rio de Janeiro introduces biometric birth registration for mothers and newborns

Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state has authorized maternity hospitals to collect fingerprints from mothers and newborns within 24 hours of birth, linking the biometric records to civil birth registration. The initiative is intended to reduce baby-swapping, illegal adoption and child trafficking, Brazilian outlet g1 reports.

The framework was established by Provision CGJ 90/2026, issued by the Rio de Janeiro Court of Justice on November 17.

Brazil recorded an average of 66 missing children and adolescents per day in 2025, according to Ministry of Justice data. The figure covers minors generally, rather than cases of newborns abducted from hospitals.

The Maternity School at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) began collecting biometrics from mothers and newborns within 24 hours of birth in October, according to g1.

The report quotes an official with Brazil’s civil registration authority as saying the early inclusion of biometric data will benefit the country’s CRVS system.

The measure applies to maternity hospitals with notary offices, of which there are 58 in Rio de Janeiro. Officials hope to introduce the process at the first 15 of them by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

Rio de Janeiro is the first Brazilian state to establish statewide rules linking newborn fingerprint collection in maternity hospitals to civil birth registration.

The initiative is led by the Rio de Janeiro Court of Justice, which also stores the biometric data.

Brazil’s infant biometrics market expands

The 1990 Child and Adolescent Statute (ECA), which is separate from the Digital ECA that mandates online age assurance, requires Brazil’s states to accurately identify children and their mothers.

Nine states in Brazil had begun registering infant biometrics using fingerprint scanners from Infant.ID as of July, according to CNN Brazil.

Infant.ID technology has also been undergoing testing at UFRJ’s Maternity School to assess its integration with birth registration. The company supplies the technology behind Paraná’s Bebê ID program, launched in 2025, although Rio’s new framework has not been formally identified as an extension of that initiative.

Infant.ID is a subsidiary of Akiyama that uses technology from Integrated Biometrics, and IB also holds the license for the technology outside Brazil. The company said last July that it had already completed more than 320,000 biometric fingerprint enrollments of children between birth and seven years of age.

Synolo is also active in Brazil’s infant fingerprint biometrics market, having signed deals with three distributors in the country last year. One of those, Montreal, is active in Rio de Janeiro and recently demonstrated its own ABIS paired with Synolo’s Neo device to state officials.

“Rio’s proposed infant biometrics provision has the potential to set a national standard for Brazil, and it aligns perfectly with what the Synolo Neo was designed to do,” Greg Scott, CEO of Synolo Biometrics, told Biometric Update in an email.

The company has completed or ongoing PoCs in eight Brazilian states, according to Scott.

Article Topics

Autism diagnoses have climbed to levels that should have triggered a national reckoning years ago. The numbers continue to rise, families are searching for answers, and the explanations offered to parents have become increasingly difficult to reconcile with the changes they are witnessing in their own children. Julie Lapidus spent more than 16 years investigating this growing crisis, and her findings raise serious questions about the environmental exposures children encounter during the most vulnerable stages of brain development.

I have spent more than 26 years researching vaccines and their potential consequences. When I began, autism prevalence was estimated at approximately one in 150 children. Today, the commonly cited figure is one in 31. Julie’s investigation challenges the assumption that improved diagnosis adequately explains this increase. Her research led her into historical cases of neurological injury caused by toxic exposure, including the mercury poisoning associated with the hat-making industry and the devastating events at Minamata Bay in Japan. The neurological symptoms documented in these cases prompted her to investigate a connection she had initially been reluctant to consider.

That investigation eventually brought her to thimerosal, the mercury-containing preservative once widely used in childhood vaccines. Julie describes discovering discrepancies between public statements about its removal and the continued distribution of multidose influenza vaccines. She purchased commercial sales data after struggling to obtain reliable information about the number of doses potentially involved. Her findings raised questions about the accuracy of publicly reported figures, particularly when she compared industry sales information with CDC distribution estimates. The difference was substantial, and the underlying discrepancy remained unexplained.

The concerns extend to aluminum exposure during childhood. Julie examined changes in the vaccination schedule and calculated potential cumulative exposure to aluminum-containing vaccine formulations. She also investigated a published criticism of the risk calculations used in evaluating aluminum exposure. The possibility of combined exposure to mercury and aluminum adds another dimension to the scientific questions she raises. These are complex toxicological issues, particularly when exposure occurs during periods of rapid neurological development and the available measurements are interpreted differently.

Her book, The Autism Generation: Understanding the Autism Epidemic from Causes to Solutions, introduces a model she calls neurodisruption. It examines the possibility that accumulated chemical exposures interfere with communication between neurons and glial cells during development. Julie connects this proposed mechanism to research involving neuroinflammation and microglial activation. Her argument places considerable attention on the interaction between environmental exposures and genetic susceptibility, leaving important questions about causation and individual vulnerability unresolved.

For parents already facing an autism diagnosis, the investigation becomes deeply personal. Julie’s younger brother’s experience with autism shaped her commitment to finding practical approaches that families could explore. The discussion turns toward nutritional deficiencies, food sensitivities, and dietary interventions that some families report finding helpful. I also share an experience from my clinical practice involving a child with severe behavioral difficulties and suspected food sensitivities. These accounts raise further questions about the medical and nutritional assessments children receive before treatment decisions are made.

The research is extensive, the implications deserve scrutiny, and some of the most consequential questions remain unanswered. This is a conversation that deserves your full attention, especially if you have been told the investigation is already settled.

Meet the Guest

Julie Lapidus is the founder and CEO of Autism Evolution and author of The Autism Generation: Understanding the Autism Epidemic from Causes to Solutions. Her younger brother’s experience with autism inspired more than 16 years of research into neurodevelopment, environmental exposures, and biomedical approaches. With two Master of Science degrees and additional training in holistic health and complementary therapies, Julie has examined historical toxicological cases, vaccine ingredients, and emerging research into brain inflammation. Her book brings together her personal experience and extensive investigation, including a practical guide for families navigating autism and related developmental challenges.

The Autism Generation: Understanding the Autism Epidemic from Causes to Solutions

Transcript Summary of this podcast episode ⤵

When a child stops using words they once knew, the family wants to know what happened. They also want to know what they can do tomorrow morning. Julie Lapidus understands both questions. Her younger brother’s experience with autism drove years of research and eventually became the impetus for *The Autism Generation*. The book’s strongest message is that families should never have to wait for an explanation before getting help.

Lapidus is unconvinced that better recognition tells the whole story of rising autism diagnoses. She sees a role for genetics and wants more attention paid to what children encounter during development. Her inquiry took an unlikely route, from reading about mercury poisoning among hatmakers to studying the industrial contamination that devastated Minamata, Japan. Those histories show what toxic exposure can do. Similarities between symptoms cannot tell us whether two conditions share a cause.

The book takes up thimerosal and aluminum in vaccines and asks how regulators assess exposure over time. Families deserve clear answers about what is in a vaccine and how its safety is studied. Those questions should be kept distinct from claims about what caused a child’s autism. Large studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

The most useful shift in Lapidus’s book comes when she turns to daily life. A child who eats only a handful of foods may be having a harder time than anyone realizes. Before cutting out familiar foods, families can ask a clinician whether sensory needs, digestive discomfort, or nutritional deficiencies are making meals harder. A parent’s observations can help guide that conversation.

An autistic child does not have to become someone else for life to get better. A less stressful meal, a new way to communicate, or a school day that doesn’t end in exhaustion can matter enormously. There is no deadline on that kind of progress.

Autism is a hot topic these days, and no doubt it is because nearly one out of 30 children have been diagnosed with a neurodevelop developmental disorder. In this new book by Julie Lapidus, The Autism Generation Understanding the Autism Epidemic from Causes to Solutions is likely the most comprehensive book ever written on this topic. If you have a child, a grandchild, a niece, a nephew, or a neighbor who has autism, you don’t want to miss this today’s conversation. It’s going to really, really be important.

And so is this book. Welcome to the Tenpenny Files, everyone. My name is Dr. Sherri Tenpenny, and I’m your host. If it matters to your body, your freedom, or your future, we talk about it here.

And there’s a new topic every day. So please join us daily. I want to introduce you to topics you’ve never heard of before, even controversial topics that will make you think, stretch your boundaries. We talk about politics, history, archaeology, food, farming, travel, health and health policy.

And at least once a week, I talk to pastors and authors who write about faith and biblical principles. So join me here every day, Monday through Friday at 3 p.m. Eastern on AmericaOutloud.news and iHeartRadio to listen to The Tenpenny Files, to hear from voices who’ve often been ignored, silenced, or censored. Before we begin today’s episode, I want to encourage everyone to become a 10penny prime member. Your membership supports us and helps us to be able to do the things that we do for all of you.

Please go to primemembership.dr10penny.com, Prime Membership.dr T E N P E N N Y dot com to learn about us, to learn about the program. Hopefully you’ll you can afford $25 a month to support our work. And I hope to see you there soon. And one last thing, thank you so much and welcome to our regulars.

And for our first time lesson listeners, we’re grateful that you’re here too. And we hope you’ll make us a regular stop in your day. So now with that, let’s get started. Today’s conversation is with Julie Lapidus, author of The Autism Generation, Understanding the Autism Epidemic with From Causes to Solutions, a sweeping exploration of one of today’s most urgent public health issues.

Julie weaves together memoir, science, and practical guidance to examine the rise of autism, its potential causes, and integrative approaches for prevention and recovery. Julie, welcome so much to the Tenpenny Files. I’m so happy to have this conversation with you here today. Thank you.

I’m honored to be here. Thank you so much for having me on your show today, Dr. Tenpenny. I’ve been in autism circles for the 26 years that I’ve been doing vaccine education. And when I first started doing this, autism was one in 150, which I thought was a despicable stat.

And I remember when Dr. Stephanie Senna first said that autism in boys would be one in two or 50% of the population by 2032. And the world was shocked and nothing has changed. And now we’re at one in 31 and 1 in 12 approximately boys in California. Why do people still think these numbers are due to a better diagnosis?

I really, it’s hard to say because there’s so much information now. If you really look at the research, it I think it’s it’s really hard to say. Even if you talk to teachers, who have been in the education field for over several decades, they notice a change in the schools. So I’m not sure.

I guess it’s because that’s what the news and the media say, the legacy media. But that based on my research and my findings, I would say that’s not accurate. UC Davis actually did a study in 2005, nine, in 2009, and they found they looked at a number of different factors. They looked at is the rate of autism prevalence changing due to changes in diagnostics, better, better diagnosis.

Is it because of migration patterns to California or something else? And they ultimately concluded that it was an environmental factor, and that was back in 2009. So, the research is there to show that it can’t really be just changes of diagnosis. It was a very small percentage that they could actually attribute to those factors, actually.

So and also it can’t just be genetics, right? Because genetic disorder by definition, and this is the official definition, it can’t increase by more than 1% over 100 years. And autism has gone up by over 32,000 percent from 1970 to to 2025. So that’s over about a 50-year time span.

So that’s much higher than 1%. So therefore it can’t be just genetic. Yeah, you you write a lot about, and you just mentioned total toxic burden of environmental toxicities. How do they accumulate and where do they come from?

I mean, we talk about like seed oils and and and glyphosate and pesticides. What other environmental toxicities do you have you researched in a part of your book? Yeah, that’s a great question. So total body load is a big issue.

And Dr. Patricia Lemer, oh, sorry, her name’s just Patricia Lemer, I apologize. She she wrote a book called the Total Load Theory that came out last year, and she talks a lot about this. But yeah, I think that, over time, multiple environmental factors they build up in your body, and your body can only handle so much before eventually you start to have some health issues. And I think that just is commonsensical if you think about it.

But there are a lot of factors that can affect someone’s health, right? Like electromagnetic radiation, xenobiotics, which are foreign chemicals, neurotoxins are a big issue. And in particular for autism and the potential factors, vaccines is a big issue because of the neurotoxins and xenobiotics contained within them. But there’s a lot of factors, right?

Pesticides, glyphosate exposure, antibiotics. There’s probably a list of at least 20 different factors that, can affect us. I’ve often said it’s amazing that any child gets born and is and lives to be, five years of age these days, with as much of an insult as or an assault that’s on them, not only moms that are pregnant and the the all the ultrasounds that are done and amniocentesis and prenatal monitoring and moms getting getting vaccines while they’re pregnant, and on and on. And recently, I would say it’s a it’s probably two, three months ago now, there was a big announcement about Tylenol and autism.

And I actually had Dr. William Parker on the show who wrote the book, Tylenol and Autism, and he talked about how much professional grief that he’s gotten and that he’s been trying to bring this this these connections out for several years. He said, and I asked him how certain he was of the connection, and he said, like 99.9%. And he’s taken so much professional grief over this. When you tried to get out, because your book is massive, it’s 560 pages for the audience, and it’s a huge platform.

Have you had a lot of professional grief by the things that you’ve written in your book? You mean like negative comments? Yeah. Some, not too bad, I would say.

But like there were, yeah, there were some, especially like some of the interviews that were somewhat viral, I suppose. They tend to get more negative comments, but that’s just, I guess, because there’s more people watching it. So I guess that’s to be expected. And and I got a couple of bad reviews on Goodreads and Amazon and Barnes and Noble’s like one-star review.

That’s not a good idea. What I think those one star reviews are, honestly, is I think that there is a pharma bot, a pharma troll, that that any book that comes out that says anything other than pharmaceuticals are great and vaccines don’t cause autism. They all the books get one-star reviews just because it pulls down. If you have one one star review and 55-star reviews, it still pulls down your reviews.

It’s just amazing how they work that out. It and I think that truly that that is that that it’s that it’s done intentionally just to pull the pull the ratings down. Yeah, it was it was obvious they hadn’t read the book. Some of them were just against the publisher.

They they just said they didn’t like the publisher, so I was like, great. Seriously, people in your book, you talk about that 90% of brain development occurs in the last trimester of pregnancy in the first two years of life, which is the period you call brain sculpting. And this is a time when the largest number of vaccines are given to these children. Why were you initially skeptical about the connection between vaccines and autism?

Oh, can you repeat the last sentence? I think I misheard one part of it. You were initially skeptic, skeptical about the connection between vaccines and autism. Why is that?

Oh, yeah. So originally I wanted to become a biomedical researcher to find a cure for autism and Alzheimer’s using vaccines, actually. That was my whole career goal. And I even applied to programs for PhD MD programs out of high school.

And it took it took a lot for me to open my eyes and change my mind about that career path, actually. But in in college, I actually was it’s a very unusual way I got into it, and I do talk about it in the book, but I was applying for a Watson Fellowship. So the Watson Fellowship is like this prestigious scholarship for liberal arts colleges, and you get to study a topic of your choice and travel around the world, and they like pay you to do this project for a year after college. So I applied for this Watson Fellowship, and my proposal was pretty interesting.

Like, I for some reason I wanted to look into fairy tales and environmental health cases and history for predecessors for autism. I was really interested in fairy tales growing up, so I guess that was why. And it led me down this very unusual path, and I spent like a many, many hours, like hundreds of hours researching this. But I I started looking at it led me down to looking at Mad Hatter’s disease.

So Alice in Wonderland’s Alice in Wonderland Lewis Carroll’s book, she actually supposedly lived next to Hatting Industry City. And the her character, Mad Hatter, the Mad Hatter was supposedly named after Mad Hatter’s syndrome. And so what happens when they have like these Mad Hatter shakes and issues with eye contact and irritability. And it turned out there was Mercurious nitrate vapor, I believe it was, that was they were being exposed to because they were using it to finish the felt hats.

And they were enclosed in warehouses, so they’re being overexposed to this mercury vapor. And they ended up getting Mad Hatter’s disease. And that ended up leading me to other cases of mercury poisoning. I also looked at a case of linkanthropy related to ergo, which is a fungus on on seeds, which was quite interesting.

And eventually it led me to looking at Minamata Bay disease, Minamata disease, which I’ve heard, I’m sure you’ve heard about, in tell people what that is. Tell people what that is. Yeah, so in Japan, what happened was the fish so what happened was that there’s a corporation called the Chiso Corporation, and they were dumping fertilizer into the Minnamata Bay, and the fertilizer contained levels, high levels of methylmercury. And so what’s happening is the fish were eating, were being exposed to this fertilizer, and they were ending up having high levels of mercury, and then people were eating the fish and getting mercury poisoning, and it ended up, I think it caused quite a few deaths in the area and many neurological issues and birth defects and things like that.

And so it was a pretty serious disease back then in Japan. And eventually led me to this paper that I think I want to say it was like a hundred-page paper that many different parents and researchers had put together where they compared the cases of mercury poisoning and autism and the different symptoms in different categories like GI or hearing, things like that. And they were looking at the different categories of symptoms and how they were connected and how they’re very similar. And they actually said, well, they thought that the way they were getting exposed was through vaccines.

And I couldn’t, that really surprised me because I had never heard about that, and it led me to researching it more in graduate school. But not surprisingly, I didn’t get the fellowship. But when I went to graduate school, I I was doing my master’s in sustainable development, and so my program was at a top business school in Europe, Ajusépari. And I told them the only thing I wanted to study was the usage of thymers and vaccines.

Like I was really, like, I really wanted to look into it more. And they just said, well, the only way you can look at this, we’ll let you do it, but you have to come at it from the angle of looking at the ethical crises surrounding this issue. And so that’s allowed me to write a master’s thesis on that. And I wrote like a hundred page, 50-page thesis looking at this issue, and that really started my journey on this path.

And when I turned it in, they only just gave me a grade and little other alkaline. I couldn’t believe what I had discovered because this was very, you have to understand this was before Kennedy’s book came out. This wasn’t like a big topic talked about in the news. articles.title: Mitek, FusionAuth and Identos strengthen leadership and advisory teams
articles.content:
Mitek, FusionAuth and Identos strengthen leadership and advisory teams

Digital identity companies Mitek, FusionAuth, and Identos have reported leadership and advisory appointments focused on marketing, revenue growth, and identity authorization standards.

The appointments include two C-suite executives and separate strategic advisory roles at FusionAuth and Identos for the same identity standards specialist.

Mitek appoints chief marketing officer

Mitek has appointed Laura Apel chief marketing officer, effective November 16, 2026. She will oversee global brand strategy, demand generation, product marketing, and communications.

Apel most recently led global marketing for Ericsson-owned Vonage’s API business. She previously held marketing leadership roles at Mitto and Telesign, bringing experience in communications technology and digital identity.

Her appointment follows the company’s recent hiring of Aaron Seyler as chief revenue officer. Seyler previously worked at Vonage and Telesign and now oversees Mitek’s global sales, partnerships and revenue operations.

FusionAuth names new CRO and strategic advisor

FusionAuth has appointed Phil Allen chief revenue officer and Eve Maler strategic advisor to strengthen its commercial leadership and identity standards expertise.

Allen will manage global sales, partnerships, sales engineering, and customer success. He joins from IDnow, where he served as chief commercial officer.

The appointment comes as FusionAuth reports 72 percent growth in European annual recurring revenue over two years, with the region now accounting for more than 30 percent of its total ARR.

Maler, a former ForgeRock CTO and founding chair of the SAML standards effort, will advise FusionAuth on product direction and identity standards, including authorization for AI agents acting on behalf of customers.

Identos appoints identity standards specialist Eve Maler

Identos has named Eve Maler strategic advisor, two days after FusionAuth announced her appointment to a similar role. The two advisory positions are separate, with Maler continuing her independent consulting work through Venn Factory. She will advise the Canadian company on authorization, consent and identity standards, including its work in healthcare and the public sector.

Her advisory work will support PolicyArc, Identos’ policy-based access control platform for enterprise applications and AI agents.

articles.title: Helix makes the case for voice age estimation backed by independent testing
articles.content:
Helix makes the case for voice age estimation backed by independent testing

Helix is a U.S. startup that uses locally processed voice biometrics to assess proof of personhood and provide age assurance.

The company’s tech uses voice biometrics to analyze a four-digit vocal challenge, providing biometric assurance that the user is a live person, along with an estimation of the speaker’s age. The tech can also be used for biometric authentication. Helix says the biometric data is processed on-device in less than four seconds.

The company has come out of the gate with $6.2 million in pre-seed funding, a board including Ticketmaster executive Jared Smith, and several independent certifications. Helix has received certification under the IEEE Online Age Verification Certification Program and has also been independently assessed by the Age Check Certification Scheme (ACCS) against ISO/IEC 27566-1. It was among eight providers recently identified as meeting New York SAFE for Kids Act accuracy requirements.

Alex Oberg, CEO of Helix, tells the Biometric Update Podcast that Helix considers itself a research lab, “with voice being the predominant biometric. One way to think about that is identity. Another is age assurance. I would argue there’s security plays. There’s even healthcare plays.”

Helix’s pitch sounds utopian, say four words and we can tell you’re a real person, and how old you are, and maybe a lot more, but independent testing provides evidence for its age estimation claims, while the broader potential of voice biometrics remains to be demonstrated. “I was doing the same research everyone else was doing,” Oberg says, “and I knew that people would be skeptical if we came out with these claims surrounding voice and we didn’t have the independent authority to back it up.”

Listen to the full conversation on the Biometric Update Podcast to hear Oberg discuss how Helix evaluates voice-based age estimation, why local processing matters for privacy, and what independent certification can establish about emerging biometric technologies.

articles.content:
Apache Roller unauthenticated code execution in XML-RPC endpoint

9.8CriticalCNA

  • Exploited
  • Yes, on CISA KEV
  • Fix
  • Fixed in 6.1.5
  • Who is exposed

Summary

Apache Roller has a deserialization flaw in its XML-RPC endpoint that lets a remote attacker run arbitrary code on the server without logging in. The endpoint deserializes vendor extension types before it checks the requester's identity.

Written by a model

Original description

Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.

This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited.

Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.

articles.title: identifAI secures €2.5M EU grant for deepfake detection technology
articles.content:
identifAI secures €2.5M EU grant for deepfake detection technology

Italian deepfake detection firm identifAI is among 35 companies selected for a €2.5 million grant through the European Innovation Council (EIC) Accelerator, with the possibility of up to €10 million in additional equity investment, subject to an assessment by the EIC Fund.

The selection followed a competitive evaluation involving 453 full applications, with 88 companies advancing to interviews. Of the 35 selected, 32 will be assessed for potential equity investment.

The list of selected companies formally credits identifAI’s “next generation synthetic media forensic detector and threat intelligence platform.”

“This selection is an important milestone for IdentifAI and a strong recognition of the work our team has been carrying out,” says Marco Ramilli, CEO of identifAI. “We are proud to bring European technological innovation to the international stage and contribute to the development of technologies addressing one of the most pressing challenges of the AI era.”

The EIC’s own announcement says companies were selected for their “transformative technologies and strong commercial promise.”

The final list includes companies from 17 EU and associated countries, with the highest number coming from France, Switzerland and Germany. Thirty-one percent of the companies are led by women in key leadership roles.

The EIC has proposed €84 million in grants for the 35 selected companies. Grant agreements are expected to be finalized within three months.

As well as financial support, the EIC Accelerator supports high-risk, high-potential startups and SMEs with access to international investors, industry leaders and business acceleration services.

articles.title: NYPD facial recognition oversight gaps exposed after 26,000 searches
articles.content:
NYPD facial recognition oversight gaps exposed after 26,000 searches

The New York Police Department’s Facial Identification Section conducted approximately 26,000 facial recognition analyses in 2025, while another police unit made nearly 100 approved requests to Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for searches against outside image repositories, according to a new watchdog report identifying gaps in oversight and disclosure.

The report, released by the New York City Department of Investigation’s Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD found that although the department “largely” complies with the city’s Public Oversight of Surveillance Technology Act (POST Act), it violated some departmental policies and failed to meet certain legal requirements.

Investigators issued 17 recommendations.

The NYPD uses three facial recognition products using different algorithms and image repositories. DataWorks Face Plus searches New York and New Jersey arrest photographs, DataWorks+ PhotoManager searches NYPD arrest photographs, including juvenile images and Idemia’s FaceExpert searches adult NYPD arrest photographs.

Investigators identified seven searches of juvenile arrest photographs between November 2025 and January 2026.

The department’s publicly posted Facial Recognition Impact and Use Policy identifies the vendors but not their individual products, contrary to POST Act disclosure requirements.

NYPD logs identified 98 approved requests between October 2023 and October 2025 for facial recognition searches outside departmental repositories. All originated with the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau and were referred to CBP.

Investigators found that the approvals did not follow the departmental policy then in force. Records contained no denied requests and little explanation of why searches were authorized.

The report does not identify which CBP platforms or image repositories were used, leaving unanswered whether NYPD photographs were searched against federal law enforcement, immigration, border security or commercial databases.

CBP has integrated Clearview AI into intelligence operations. The watchdog report, however, does not establish that Clearview was used for any of the 98 NYPD referrals.

The investigation followed an August 2025 Legal Aid Society complaint alleging that NYPD personnel circumvented restrictions by using outside agencies.

In one case, an NYPD investigator enlisted a New York City Fire Department official to conduct a Clearview AI search involving a pro-Palestinian demonstrator. A judge subsequently found that the search “clearly contravene[d] official NYPD policy.”

The watchdog recommended formal authorization procedures and auditable records for searches conducted through outside agencies.

NYPD policy requires human peer review and supervisory approval before facial recognition candidates are forwarded to investigators.

While matches serve as investigative leads, not independent grounds for arrest, approximately 33 percent of Intelligence Division searches recorded during 2024 and 2025 were marked as receiving no supervisory review. The watchdog noted ambiguity in the department’s written requirements but recommended consistent supervisory approval of potential matches.

Investigators also found authorized police units failed to document peer reviews, making compliance difficult to verify. Separate recordkeeping systems created risks of duplicate searches and conflicting results.

The NYPD said it has since consolidated Intelligence Division searches within its Regional Intelligence Support Center and moved requests into a centralized case management system.

Investigators found NYPD facial recognition products contain image-editing tools exceeding those permitted under current policy, including a paintbrush feature and the ability to export photographs for external editing.

Officials acknowledged that some former Facial Identification Section investigators had used extensive image-editing techniques, although they said current personnel do not.

The City Council subsequently enacted Local Law 55 of 2025, requiring records of image modifications, preservation of original and altered photographs, and annual facial recognition audits. The NYPD had rejected similar watchdog recommendations in 2022.

The report also found no routine process for reviewing updated National Institute of Standards and Technology evaluations of the department’s facial recognition algorithms, despite potential changes in accuracy and demographic performance following vendor updates.

The privacy advocacy group Surveillance Technology Oversight Project renewed its call for a ban on police facial recognition, citing the volume of searches and CBP collaboration.

The NYPD maintains that it does not use real-time facial recognition and that matches alone cannot justify an arrest.

The watchdog’s findings expose a large, increasingly interconnected biometric surveillance operation whose oversight and disclosure mechanisms have not consistently kept pace with its use.

Article Topics

biometric matching | biometrics | facial recognition | NYPD | video surveillance

articles.title: COVID testing claims and the case against Ron Elfenbein
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | RSS

Remember sitting in your car waiting for a COVID-19 test so you could go back to work? In Maryland, Dr. Ron Elfenbein helped get drive-up testing off the ground. His urgent care operation grew from one location to eight. Federal officials even asked him to help open an antibody infusion site at FedEx Field. Then the Justice Department accused him of fraud.

Prosecutors said his practice submitted more than $15 million in false claims to Medicare and a private insurer. They alleged that he directed staff to bill for high-level evaluations that patients who came for tests did not receive. A jury convicted him on five counts. Then the judge who heard the evidence wrote a 93-page opinion acquitting him, finding that the government hadn’t met its burden. Prosecutors appealed, clearing the way for another trial.

Elfenbein says a coding expert reviewed hundreds of charts and backed the practice’s billing. The American Medical Association weighed in on the billing rules in a friend-of-the-court brief. And that $15 million figure? It’s what prosecutors say was billed, not what Elfenbein personally pocketed. That distinction matters when a dollar figure is big enough to drown out everything else.

Elfenbein had publicly blasted the Biden administration for restricting access to monoclonal antibody treatments. He suspects the prosecution was payback. The timing doesn’t prove it, and he says he can’t prove it. What we do know is that a federal judge heard the same case the jury heard and found the evidence insufficient.

Pandemic fraud deserves prosecution. That doesn’t justify putting a doctor through another criminal trial over disputed billing when the first trial ended with that finding. The Justice Department should drop the case. And when we vote, we ought to remember that holding government accountable includes asking how it uses its power against the people who criticize it.

It’s 6 Eastern. It’s 3 o’clock Pacific. This is a president of action. Coast to coast and around the world from the America Out Loud Talk Radio Studios.

If he says he’s serious about something, he means it. It’s time for The Truth Be Told with Booker Scott. Out of all the fraud and abuse that I’ve seen over the last five or six years, I think the one that bothers me the most is what happened during COVID. You had $500 billion to $1 trillion in fraud.

Most of it was through unemployment fraud, PPP, but these people were getting away with stealing billions of dollars. The Department of Justice has tried, and they have successfully brought back some of that money, but not much. And we’re never going to see it all back. It’s impossible.

We see that this week, Sheila She Philas McCormick, a congresswoman from the state of Florida, she resigned for allegedly stealing $5.6 million. But it wasn’t just Democrats. There was also George Santos, the Republican that got expelled from Congress. And he did the same thing.

Not $5.6 million, but he stayed on unemployment even though he was continuing to work all through COVID. He got unemployment benefits. I saw one last week. It was a former pastor in Jacksonville, Florida.

He stole $50,000 in an unemployment. And that really bothered me during that time. And it still does, really. It really does.

I have a story for you here. It comes from the state of Maryland, and this happened during COVID as well. But this is not PPP and unemployment. Back then, we had all the testing sites and things like that.

I’m going to get into the story here for you tonight. We’re going to dig deep into it. I’m Booker. This is The Truth Be Told.

As we start this hour, I’m just going to read directly from the Department of Justice media release. Here’s what they said. A federal jury in Baltimore convicted a Maryland doctor for submitting over $15 million in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare and a commercial insurer for patients who received COVID-19 tests at his testing sites. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Dr. Ron Elfenbein of Maryland was an owner and the medical director of Doctors Urgent Care, and this was in Annerondo County and Prince George County in Maryland.

I’ll continue reading directly from this. They say that in addition to billing for COVID-19, he instructed the employees of Doctor’s Urgent Care that in addition to billing COVID-19 tests, the employees were to bill for high-level evaluation and management visits. In reality, these visits were not provided to patients as presented. Rather, Elfenbein instructed his employees that the patients were there for one reason only.

To be tested. That was it. Simple and straightforward. And the providers were not there to solve complex medical issues.

Elfenbein ordered these high-level visits to be billed for all patients, including those who were asymptomatic, who were getting tested for COVID-19 for their employment requirements, and who were being tested for COVID 19 so that they could travel. Remember those days? Well, Elfenbein, through Doctors Urgent Care, caused the submission of millions of dollars in claims to Medicare and a commercial insurer for tens of thousands of dollars. The interesting part of this story, and the reason why I want to bring it to you tonight, is that the judge who was appointed by Barack Obama he wrote a ninety-three-page acquittal overruling the jury.

And that doesn’t happen to have a judge come back on the jury and say, I don’t accept that. There isn’t enough evidence. And that’s exactly what happened in this case. I have talked to Dr. Ron Elfenbein, and I want to bring him back here tonight so he can tell his story to you.

And you make the decision. What do you think? The government is still going to try him, they say, after the acquittal. The government appealed, and the appellate court said, Well, you can try him again.

But they didn’t really have a problem with what the judge did in acquitting him. That’s allowed. It just never happens. But it happened in this case.

It’s a fascinating story. And it’s one I want to bring you tonight. And we’re going to do that right now. We’re going to welcome to the program Dr. Ron Elfenbein.

Dr. Elfenbein, welcome to the program. Great to have you. Thank you so much, Brooke. It’s a pleasure to be here.

Thank you. Let’s get started with the story. And I think the story is most important to tell from its beginning. And let’s talk about where that starts.

Because with you as an emergency room doctor, I believe it starts when you got into the urgent care business. And maybe it starts a little bit before that, or a little bit after that. I guess it started in about 2019 when you saw the videos from China. But let’s start at the very beginning when you got into the urgent care business.

Okay, well, going a little bit farther back. So just a little bit about me. I grew up in New York. I trained at Johns Hopkins for emergency medicine.

And I moved to Maryland to do my training at Hopkins, and I met my wife there. And she’s also a physician, and we decided to stay. So while I was a resident, I was very active with the Secret Service. I did a lot of work with the United States Secret Service.

I did some work with NASA and I did I volunteered on the Navajo Indian Reservation and I volunteered in a month at the Johnson Space Center, doing doing some pretty work on managing airway emergencies in space, which was incredible. And then in 2006, so I moved, lived in Maryland after I finished my residency in 03, and I I, as you said, opened up an urgent care center in 2016. And I was the medical director of it. I didn’t actually work there, but I was the medical director, and I hired nurse practitioners and PAs to work there.

And I just, made sure everything was going smoothly and well and set the policies and things like that, but I didn’t actually see patients. So then in 2019, also let me interrupt real quick because you also weren’t the money behind it either, were you? Not solely. You had some backers in those urgent cares.

Well, it was one urgent care, and I had two partners, and they they were they were the non they were non-phys, or they are non-physicians. I was the only doctor, and they were the they were the business side. I was the medical side, they were the business side. That’s it.

A lot of those urgent cares are set up that way, and maybe people don’t know that, but you have a doctor who is the medical director that they need, and then nurse practitioners and PAs, physician assistants, they’re the ones that actually are seeing us when we go into an urgent care. But you also have the money behind the business, and that’s the way yours was set up when you started with one one location. Correct. Yes.

And and they they it wasn’t just just the money. I mean, we were equal partners with that regard, but they they did provide a substantial amount of the money, but but it was also their job to run the business side. So it they made a very distinct line in our business plan down the middle, where anything medical would would be my purview and anything non-medical was their purview. And I we didn’t we really tried to stay out of each other’s lanes.

Yeah. That was our famous quote. Stay in your lane, stay in your lane. Yeah, they’re paying the bills, is what they’re doing.

Exactly. Yeah, exactly. So to your point, I I started to watch the news in 2019. And oh I had grown my family by then.

By the way, we had four children, and I I started to watch the news and I could see what was happening in China. And despite what our government was telling us, don’t worry about it, it’s not coming here, everything’s fine. I could see with my own two eyes what was happening. And I said, there’s no possible way.

You’re talking about COVID, and those are the videos that we all watched if we’re on social media. Not many of them made their way to the mainstream media, but we’re talking about the videos that showed people being welded into their apartments that happened, fumigating subways, and it really looked terrible. And of course, I’ve always said that the only thing that gets out of China that the CCP will allow it are things that they want it to. So you can read into that what you want to, but but that’s what you’re watching.

You’re watching the same videos that I am, and probably a lot of people that are listening to this. You’re seeing those videos in 2019, which was the fall of 2019, is about when all of that started. We were watching that here in America, and we thought it was crazy, but you had a little bit of a different thought there, didn’t you? Yeah, I I mean, I to your point.

I mean, there were videos I remember clearly of literal like tanks, actual military tanks in the streets with their turrets pointed into the city to keep people in their homes and in the city. And I was like, there’s no way that this thing is contained. So I started to purchase PPE, personal protective equipment, and I started to purchase testing supplies. And everybody thought, including my wife, thought I was insane.

They’re like, What are you doing? Why are you wasting your time? And none of this stuff was easy to get, by the way. So I would spend hours and hours and hours on the phone trying to get as whatever I could get my hands on because when were you doing that?

What part was that in the 2009? 2019. Okay, and then and yeah, and then that continued, by the way, throughout the entirety of the pandemic. Getting supplies was one of the most difficult things.

And I I spent hours every single day, gloves, gowns, masks, booties, testing supplies, you name it, you disinfectant, hand sanitizer, whatever it was. It was hours every day trying to find this stuff. And once you found a supplier, it was like, at one point we couldn’t get gloves. We actually arranged to get a shipment, an entire pallet of gloves from somewhere in China.

We found a place that had them, and we bought hundreds of thousands of gloves because we just could not get them. And we literally had an entire pallet, like I don’t know, 50,000, 100,000 pairs of gloves, something ridiculous, shipped over to us because that’s all we could find. So you started the process in 2019, in the fall of 2019. And the pandemic really starts in March of 2020.

2020. Yeah, and that’s about when things shut down here in America. By the time that happened, how much had you stockpiled at that time of PPE and all of this other equipment? I honestly don’t remember, but I know our store our like our storehouses, were full, and we actually had to go and get a another warehouse.

Right down the street from the urgent care is a storage facility, like an off-site storage place. Yeah, sure. And we rented, we rented a storage unit there, and we would use we would use that as our storage. And and well, once this all hit, I I realized I had this commodity that people needed, and I started to give it away.

I was thinking about it. I didn’t charge anybody for it. I was giving away mountains of PP to nursing homes, to other doctors. I had a friend of mine in New York who’s a cardiologist, and he got drafted, so to speak, to work in the ICU at Columbia Presbyterian in Manhattan.

I remember that. And he he he called me and he’s like, I don’t know what the hell I’m doing. How do I not die from COVID? So I went through, what to do and for hours on the phone with him.

And then he told me, he’s like, We are wearing hefty bags, literally garbage bags for our gowns. And I said, Todd, his name is Todd, I will send you a package tomorrow to share with everybody.
