articles.title: Ninth Circuit Weighs xAI Challenge to California AI Disclosure Law
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

The Ninth Circuit heard arguments in Pasadena on Wednesday in a case where xAI is trying to block a California law that requires developers of generative AI to publish a summary of the data used to train their systems.

The core question is whether a state can make a company publish information about how it built its product – and whether that is a case of compelled speech that is protected by the First Amendment.

The law, AB 2013, was signed in 2024 and came into force on January 1, 2026. It makes companies behind generative AI models disclose whether the data used to build them includes personal information, as well as other details, in order to give consumers information about the data and processes behind the models.

The law applies to models released on or after January 1, 2022, and the first disclosure was required by January 1 of this year. Another is due before each new release or substantial modification of the model.

The law states that the disclosure can be a “high-level summary” and can include data-point counts in “general ranges.”

The information that must be disclosed includes whether the data used to train the model contains personal information, as defined in the law; whether it contains data protected by copyright, trademark, or patent; whether the data was purchased or licensed; the sources or owners of the data; and whether synthetic data was used.

The law exempts systems whose sole purpose is to help ensure security and integrity, as well as aircraft operation, and those made available to a federal entity for national security purposes.

The law was challenged by xAI in a lawsuit filed in December 2025, which argued, in the district court's summary, that it “violates the First Amendment by compelling Plaintiff’s speech based on content and viewpoint.”

The viewpoint claim is based on the fact that the law exempts systems that have to do with security, aircraft operation, and national security.

xAI also said that information about the datasets and processes AI developers use to train their AI models is “a closely protected trade secret.”

The law also has a privacy component that is hard to argue against: the public has a stake in knowing whether their personal data was used to train an AI model.

As for the hearing on Wednesday, reports say that xAI got a “cold reception” from the three-judge panel, although it was not a uniformly negative experience for the company.

According to MLex, the panel – consisting of Judges Johnnie Rawlinson, Smith, and Forrest – “pressed” both xAI and the state of California.

The argument lasted 46 minutes, but there has been no decision yet.

Rawlinson asked, according to Bloomberg Law, “Isn’t it reasonable for the government to want its citizens to be able to know upfront what information is being input” into AI models.

The argument that xAI is making is that this is compelled speech – and that it is not justified by a compelling government interest.

In March, US District Judge Jesus Bernal denied xAI a preliminary injunction. The company had already, on December 30, 2025, posted a “high-level, limited disclosure that does not reveal its trade secrets.”

Bernal said that xAI had “failed at this stage to sufficiently allege that trade secrets are implicated.”

Bernal found that AB 2013 was likely a content-based rule, but one that is “commercial speech” – and therefore subject to intermediate scrutiny under the Central Hudson standard, rather than strict scrutiny.

He also rejected xAI’s claim that the data is useless to consumers, saying, “It strains credulity to essentially suggest that no consumer is capable of making a useful evaluation of Plaintiff’s AI models by reviewing information about the datasets used to train them.”

However, the judge also left the door open for xAI by stating that it had “demonstrated a distinct possibility of prevailing on the merits under Central Hudson. But it had not demonstrated a likelihood of success.”

Bernal noted that “’consumer curiosity’ alone is generally insufficient as a substantial state interest” – and distinguished the case from X Corp. v. Bonta (2024), where the Ninth Circuit blocked a different California law that tried to force social media companies to reveal their positions on “hate speech or misinformation.”

AB 2013, Bernal said, does not involve “mandatory disclosure of controversial opinions.”

Several amicus briefs were filed in support of California, including one by the Knight First Amendment Institute, whose legal fellow Stephany Kim said, “The companies building these systems shouldn’t also be the ones deciding what the public gets to know about them.”

She added that “the public knows very little about how they are built, operate, and affect our information ecosystem.”

Another group, LASST, also filed an amicus brief in support of the law, with attorney Ben Rashkovich telling Transformer, “Transparency is the floor for AI governance, not the ceiling” and “this case is about whether the First Amendment can be used to knock that floor out.”

The case is important because it will set a precedent for how far states can go in requiring AI companies to publish information about their products.

New York’s RAISE Act, that comes into force on January 1, 2027, also requires disclosures – and, as Reclaim The Net reported on November 13, adds confidential incident reports and fines. On the same day as the Ninth Circuit hearing, California Governor Gavin Newsom proposed more mandatory testing and incident reporting.

In April, a federal judge in Colorado put that state’s AI law on hold after xAI sued, arguing that the law was “an effort to embed the State’s preferred views into the very fabric of AI systems.” At the time, we wrote, “the government doesn’t get to write the script.”

The line between a state forcing a company to disclose a factual list of data sources – and a state writing the script – is what makes this issue complex.

It is also important to look at the track record of companies like xAI, who are now trying to block disclosure of data sources.

xAI’s AI assistants were also reported to have made unauthorized requests to a number of connected services.

According to a November 17 report by NewCore, a company that sells AI access controls, two of xAI’s Grok Bot assistants made 31 such calls over five days to Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, without users asking for them.

NewCore said that the API calls did not show up in the chat history of the bots, adding, “None appear in its own chat history.”

xAI reacted by adding an off switch – but left it on by default.

It’s true that the First Amendment’s protection against compelled speech is an important line that courts should guard – and it’s also true that the government should not be allowed to use “transparency” as a pretext to force companies to publish opinions scripted by the state, as was the case in X Corp. and is the case in Colorado.

For a plain, factual list of data sources, including whether personal data of citizens was used to build an AI model, it’s the citizens who have a right to know – and who have a better claim than the company that used that data in the first place.

The danger is that once the door is open, states will start demanding more and more information, using “transparency” as a battering ram, and eventually cross the line into opinion-making.

articles.title: Signal Adds Protections Against AI Agents Reading Screens
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

The latest update of the Signal app on iOS 27 and on Android is designed to block the operating systems' AI agents from reading the content of the app's screens.

This is because these agents, integrated into the operating systems, read what is on the screen, and since Signal decrypts messages in the app, the OS then has access to that content.

The fact that agents scan the screen means that "your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding," Signal explained. Once the data is captured, it is out of Signal's hands, and it exposes everyone in the conversation, not only the user: "imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation."

Signal calls this “an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”

Signal president Meredith Whittaker announced the changes in a blog post explaining that the three major OS makers, Apple, Google, and Microsoft, set the rules that all apps must follow.

Signal said that “these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim,” and that while Signal's own encryption is not broken, the message is protected only in transit, and once displayed on the screen, the OS can read it.

“This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data,” the company said.

On iOS 27, the update blocks screenshots in the app by default. On Android, the update detects when an AI assistant is trying to read the screen and automatically turns on the Screen security setting in Signal. However, this does not apply to all Android devices, as many vendors do not provide a reliable way to detect this.

Users can turn this setting off in Signal's settings, but the app warns that this will potentially expose Signal content to AI agents.

On macOS, Signal says it cannot block screenshots in a reliable way for lack of documented tools provided by Apple. As a workaround, macOS 27 users are advised to add Signal to Excluded Apps under System Settings > Siri.

The company admits that the measure it has taken is only a partial fix, as “restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.”

The agents in question are the likes of Apple's Siri AI, that has "onscreen awareness" and can "answer questions or take actions related to the content on a user’s screen," and Google's Gemini that can automate multi-step tasks across apps, and is "even more powerful when you add screen or image context."

There is also Meta's Muse, that has more than 10 million downloads since its launch in September, and that can, according to a report by Reuters, pull Signal messages from push notifications on Android, use accessibility and screenshot tools on a Mac, but is blocked on an iPhone.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the examples were “isolated incidents” and that the agent can access other apps only through permissions explicitly granted by users. Google said that people “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to read Android notifications.

Signal president Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse "without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity," and that its deployment was "technologically reckless."

Meanwhile, Signal's Whittaker has asked Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide developers with tools to stop their apps' data from being accessed by AI agents, and documentation on how this data is used.

Signal says it is "cautiously optimistic" about the result of its request, as Google and Apple are already in talks with the company. What Signal wants is a way for developers to opt out of AI data access, and for this to apply to screen reading, file access, notifications, and APIs.

The company also wants the three OS makers to make sure that accessibility settings are not used as a backdoor by AI agents, and to provide proper documentation of how these agents access and process data.

This is not the first time Signal has had to take steps to protect its users from OS-level AI agents. In May 2025, it turned on "Screen security" by default on Windows 11 to keep Microsoft's Recall from taking screenshots of chats every few seconds.

"Microsoft has simply given us no other option," Signal said at the time, and warned that agents could "break the blood-brain barrier between applications and operating systems."

articles.title: Gemini Chats Set to Stay on Google’s Servers Even After History Is Turned Off
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

Google has announced that the “History” setting in its Gemini app has changed in a blog post published on Monday.

This is how the change is presented in the blog: “Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months; they’re used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.”

The blog post never mentions the previous 72-hour time frame, but instead frames the announcement as giving users more control over their data.

That “off” means something entirely different now than it used to is evident from Google’s own Privacy Hub, which was updated to reflect the change.

Previously, the page said, “Temporary chats and chats you have when Keep Activity is off are retained with your account for 72 hours.”

Now, the same page states, “Temporary chats and chats you have when your History setting is off are retained with your account for around two months.”

This means that both temporary chats, and those that take place when the new History setting is turned off, will be kept by Google for a roughly 20 times longer period than before.

While the blog post tries to put a positive spin on this by emphasizing “more control,” the reality is that the off switch has changed significantly.

Not only will turning it off now hide chats from the user’s view, but Google will still keep them for two months.

This applies to Gemini Live (voice and video) chats with History off as well: previously, these were kept “up to 72 hours,” and now it’s “around two months.”

The Privacy Hub now also reveals that even if Gemini History is turned off, future chats will still be saved for around two months and used to respond to the user, process their feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public – “with help from human reviewers.”

The “human reviewers” include those from outside the company – “trained reviewers from our service providers” – and their access to chats is not limited to those taking place when the History setting is on.

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies,” the Privacy Hub warns.

If a user provides “feedback” (by giving a thumbs up or down, or reporting an issue) in a chat while History is off, Google will take “the last 24 hours of your chats” and “any content included in those chats (like attachments and data from Connected Apps).”

This data is then “retained for up to 3 years” – and is kept “disconnected from your Google Account.”

The same three-year retention period for reviewed chats, feedback, and associated files has been in place before this change, as the November 12 copy of the Privacy Hub reveals. At that time, it was stated that reviewed chats are saved for up to three years, even if a user deletes them, and that they are not deleted when history is deleted, but instead retained for up to three years.

Google’s explanation for storing chats for such a long time is that they are kept “so they are available in case of a potential system failure.”

The company has also issued a statement to reporters, saying that the reason the time has been extended from 72 hours to two months is “to detect, report, and investigate complex emerging abuse scenarios.”

Google also said that the retained data “will strictly not be used for GAI model training or for other product improvement purposes.”

The company did not define what an “abuse scenario” is, or how many chats with the History setting off are reviewed by humans.

articles.title: Former UK Minister Calls for New Censorship Law After Google Refuses Takedown
articles.content:
If you're tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net.

The British government’s request to Google to delete a video from YouTube has been turned down – but that doesn’t mean the end of the affair.

In fact, former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls Jess Phillips has now suggested that a new law may be needed to make it compulsory for the tech giant to remove the video.

“Regulatory frameworks, changes and potentially a second online safety act is needed, because before we haven’t had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings,” she said.

It was only a day ago that the government’s request was revealed, and the company said no. The video that caused the government to try to censor YouTube in this way is a message from comedian and YouTuber Russell Brand, who is currently in prison after a jury convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and sentenced him to 10 years and six months.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on the couple’s YouTube show, in which he said, “I am not guilty of the offenses I have been jailed for.”

This was the content that the government asked Google to delete, but the company found that the video did not break any of its rules.

When asked if he would change the law, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, "I wouldn't leap to that."

"I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here. Think of the victims, that's the main thing. Show some decency," he said.

According to the Ministry of Justice, “it was only right” to ask for content that was “distressing for victims” to be removed, while “removal ultimately depends on the platform’s own terms” – but “YouTube should remove this content.”

But they don’t have to. And Phillips is admitting that the government “doesn’t have the power to enforce that this video is taken down.”

And the reason is that the rules in place are “almost certainly not” the right ones to deal with this situation. “This is an entirely new era and frankly the regulations are almost certainly not in place for the government to just demand that this be taken down,” she said on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

However, this “new era” already has rules in place that cover this situation – and it is the Prison Service that is in charge here, not Google.

The Prison Service’s communications rules (PSI 49/2011, revised August 2026) bar material meant for the internet, or likely to be published there, that is about the prisoner’s own crime – “except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence.”

An investigation into whether Brand broke these rules is already under way, and Justice Secretary Alex Norris said, “I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.”

Possible penalties, according to the BBC, are a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls. In 2022, Charles Bronson reportedly had phone restrictions imposed on him after an unauthorised message to Sky News.

But this is not enough for some politicians. She even went as far as to frame it as Google’s fault that the government doesn’t have the power to make the company delete the video.

“All Google do by leaving this up is show that those codes are not good enough,” she said. And then she issued a threat: “If Google want less regulation they will take this down.”

The “codes” here refer to the voluntary Ofcom women’s safety codes. Phillips dismissed them as useless, saying, “Ofcom codes on women’s safety online are just voluntary and frankly voluntary codes to tech companies is the triumph of hope over experience.”

And she also suggested the government would look at bringing in a second Online Safety Act, saying it was “very likely.”

“Regulatory frameworks, changes and potentially a second online safety act is needed, because before we haven’t had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings,” she said.

But Ofcom itself said that its current guidance is voluntary and that “any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament.”

Meanwhile, other ministers are still reiterating that the video should be taken down. Children’s minister Josh MacAlister said he hoped Google would make the same decision as Meta – which has disabled Brand’s Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp accounts.

articles.title: WhatsApp Fixes Flaw Uncovered While Disrupting Scam Campaign
articles.content:
WhatsApp has patched a low-impact vulnerability in its Android apps that it believes a scammer may have exploited to make scam messages seem more credible.

Tracked as CVE-2026-23871, WhatsApp’s security team found the flaw. It’s tied to Click to WhatsApp ads and affects both WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android.

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread,” WhatsApp explained in its advisory.

The advisory also says the vulnerability “may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

Asked by SecurityWeek about the exploitation, a WhatsApp spokesperson said, “Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.”

WhatsApp also published advisories for two medium-impact vulnerabilities, saying it has seen no evidence that either was exploited.

One of them, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection bug affecting WhatsApp for Android versions prior to 2.26.35.74. Tapping a maliciously crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client could lead to the deletion of WhatsApp files stored on the device.

If the recipient was online when the message arrived, an attacker could also have learned one bit of information about their chat database. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s bug bounty program.

The second, CVE-2026-44908, was discovered by Meta’s own researchers. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that WhatsApp apps use to confirm they can trust Meta AI’s confidential computing backend.

Someone “positioned within Meta infrastructure” could have bypassed the hardware root of trust using a certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer’s key.

The bug impacted certain versions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for iOS and Android, as well as WhatsApp for Mac.

WhatsApp noted that such a certificate could not have been used without first being published to a third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing relies on.

“The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation,” the company said.

articles.title: AI and Governance Leadership Forum and Awards 2026 highlights responsible innovation
articles.content:
The AI and Governance Leadership Forum and Awards 2026 convened government officials, technology executives, and cybersecurity experts to address the critical need for responsible artificial intelligence adoption and robust governance frameworks, as highlighted by TahawulTech.

Hosted at The Ritz-Carlton Abu Dhabi, Grand Canal, the event focused on the transition from AI experimentation to enterprise-wide implementation. Key discussions emphasized the necessity of maintaining human oversight, transparency and cybersecurity as autonomous systems become increasingly embedded in public services and business operations. Industry leaders explored how to translate high-level AI principles into practical operating models, ensuring that innovation does not compromise accountability.

The forum featured two primary panel discussions that examined the complexities of governing agentic AI, third-party models, and non-human identities. Experts highlighted the importance of securing AI supply chains and preserving data sovereignty while balancing operational flexibility with centralized oversight. The evening concluded with an awards ceremony recognizing individuals and organizations for their contributions to digital transformation, risk management and secure AI deployment across the region.

By fostering collaboration between the public and private sectors, the event underscored that effective governance is essential for building digital trust and ensuring that intelligent technologies deliver sustainable value in an evolving technological landscape.

Source: TahawulTech

articles.title: Cato Networks introduces AgentSense to secure autonomous AI agents
articles.content:
Cato Networks has launched AgentSense, a new security solution designed to detect prompt injection attacks and prevent unauthorized actions by autonomous AI agents before they occur, according to Channel Insider.

Developed by Cato AI Labs, the tool monitors how external data influences AI decision-making. It features Untrusted Influence Detection, which separates verified instructions from potentially malicious content to block zero-day vulnerabilities. Additionally, Drift Detection ensures that an agent’s actions remain aligned with its original objectives, preventing it from straying into unsafe territory. This technology addresses growing concerns regarding the security of agentic AI in enterprise environments.

To validate the system, Cato Networks has launched a security challenge, offering $10,000 to the first three participants who successfully bypass the protection. For managed service providers and channel partners, this development represents a significant opportunity to expand service offerings. Beyond securing infrastructure, partners can now provide specialized AI governance, monitoring, and workflow integrity services.

As businesses increasingly rely on autonomous agents for critical operations, the ability to control agent behavior becomes as vital as traditional financial security. This shift allows organizations to deploy advanced AI with greater confidence while maintaining oversight of automated processes.

Source: Channel Insider

articles.title: Aureon launches Unified Protection for managed IT and cybersecurity
articles.content:
Aureon is launching Unified Protection, a new three-tier portfolio designed to integrate managed IT services with advanced cybersecurity capabilities, as reported by Channel Insider.

The portfolio combines continuous IT monitoring, 24/7 security operations, and active threat response to help organizations simplify management across devices, identities, and cloud environments. The service is structured into three tiers: Essentials, which provides core monitoring and endpoint detection and response; Defense, which adds multifactor authentication and data backup; and Resilience, which incorporates security information and event management, vulnerability management and dark web monitoring.

Joe Johnson, the vice president of product development at Aureon, noted that IT and cybersecurity must function as a single unit to provide better visibility and response capabilities. For managed service providers and channel partners, this offering creates a pathway to expand security portfolios without the need to build internal around-the-clock operations.

By utilizing this tiered model, partners can generate recurring revenue through service bundling and customer upgrades, addressing the growing market demand for integrated technology and security management. The solution allows businesses to scale their protection as their operational requirements evolve over time.

Source: Channel Insider

articles.title: Menlo Security expands AI and browser security offerings
articles.content:
Menlo Security is accelerating its efforts to protect AI agents and secure employee use of AI tools, creating new opportunities for partners as browser security becomes a top priority for organizations, as reported by CRN.

Menlo Security CEO Bill Robbins stated that the company has broadened its capabilities to defend against threats targeting both human users and autonomous agents. A primary focus is the Menlo Agent Runtime Security, or MARS, which prevents AI agents from being compromised or leaking sensitive corporate data. Additionally, the company recently unveiled the IRIS Browser Extension, which provides security controls for existing browsers without requiring a switch.

This tool supports platforms including Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox, offering protections against unauthorized data copying, printing, and file exfiltration. Menlo Security also utilizes its HEAT Shield technology, which employs a proprietary large language model to identify and block novel, highly evasive threats with 98% to 99% certainty. By focusing on prevention rather than detection, the company aims to address the rapid speed at which modern cyberattacks occur.

With annual recurring revenue reaching approximately $175 million, Menlo Security is positioning these tools as a scalable progression for partners, starting with browser extensions and moving toward comprehensive isolation and agent security solutions.

Source: CRN

articles.title: iDenfy achieves PCI DSS certification for Bank Card Verification service
articles.content:
iDenfy has secured a Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard v4.0.1 Attestation of Compliance for its Bank Card Verification service. This certification follows a rigorous assessment conducted by the Qualified Security Assessor, Trausta, UAB, as first reported by Biometric Update.

The Bank Card Verification service serves as a critical tool for fraud prevention, particularly within the igaming industry where multi-accounting remains a persistent threat. The service can function as a standalone module or as part of a broader know your customer workflow. To ensure data security, iDenfy processes card images in a dedicated environment without storing them. The system does not retain full card numbers or card verification values, logging only truncated data, cardholder names, expiration dates, and verification results.

Originally launched as a platform feature in 2024, the capability became a standalone dashboard module earlier this year. Chief Executive Officer Domantas Ciulde noted that the certification allows partners to integrate card verification alongside existing identity and anti-money laundering checks while maintaining industry-standard data protection.

Customers can implement the service through an application programming interface, iFrame, or mobile software development kit. This milestone underscores the company's commitment to building security directly into its verification products as it expands its suite of onboarding tools.

Source: Biometric Update

articles.title: In Other News: Norwegian Energy Firm Cyberattacks, Supercomputer Hack, New Nightmare Eclipse Exploit
articles.content:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights: 

Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI

AI evaluation firm Trajectory Labs says Gemini 4 Argon agents it stress-tested in October, with Gemini’s API safeguards turned on, tried to hack Epoch AI’s live website while hunting for answers to non-existent FrontierMath problems, attempting SQL injection and impersonating Epoch staff. Trajectory has paused all misalignment testing. Epoch says no private information was accessed.

Google brings Gemini 4 Neon to defenders 

Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and says a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders in the coming days. Google claims the model performs at frontier level across finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. It also says Neon keeps Carbon-level safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while turning down far fewer legitimate requests in those areas.

Compromised migration vendor opens door to Infoblox data theft

Networking and security company Infoblox has confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, which TechCrunch’s sources say handled SharePoint migration. The Register has since reported that the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved.

EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list

The Council of the EU has sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities over Russian information manipulation and cyber activity, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency, 24 of its employees, and several pro-Kremlin propagandists. Under its cyber sanctions regime, the Council also listed NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has claimed attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states.

Japanese supercomputer offline after intrusion

Japan’s Riken research institute has suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. In a November 17 notice, Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku’s operational status to break into the system’s internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users may have been exposed.

Ukraine arrests ransomware suspects, 8-Digits member extradited to US

Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, have arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that posed as IT support in calls powered by an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or get remote access software installed. Separately, Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy has appeared in US court after being extradited from Italy over his alleged role in the 8-Digits Team, an INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate accused of stealing data from US hospitals, healthcare entities and schools and making over $500 million in ransom demands. In Florida, five people were arrested in a nationwide crackdown on account-takeover fraud schemes linked to more than $54 million in losses at over 65 US financial institutions.

Test environment intrusion exposes Rakuten Securities customer data

Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities says login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, and personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment system on November 11. The exposed details include names, dates of birth, addresses, employers, withdrawal bank account numbers, and declared annual income and financial assets.

Equinor stops cyberattack as Skagerak Energi reports attempted intrusion

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says it has stopped a cyberattack against some of its IT systems that it detected on November 17, adding that production was not affected and there is no sign that data was stolen or altered. The company said the attack was not a virus attack and did not appear to be specifically targeting it. A day after Equinor’s disclosure, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on some of its IT systems, saying operations and production were not affected and there is no sign that information was leaked.

Nightmare Eclipse drops unpatched Windows lock screen escape

Researcher Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and run code as the lock screen account. The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.

Malware targets CACs left in personal computers

The NSA says threat actors are using malware against the personal computers that Department of War (DoW) employees use with Common Access Card (CAC) readers. Once the malware has recorded the card’s PIN, it can use the CAC’s credentials to sign into federal and DoW websites for as long as the card stays in the reader. That often gives attackers access to anything the cardholder can normally reach.

articles.title: US launches center to disrupt scams and warn victims sooner
articles.content:
.kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kt-inside-inner-col > .kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > }@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column491337_ded6e7-0b > }

In this article

  • The Threat Disruption Center brings investigators and companies together to disrupt criminal networks targeting Americans
  • It aims to help warn victims sooner, interrupt payments, and take down scam infrastructure
  • If you’ve been scammed, report it promptly to the FBI’s IC3; don’t wait for the center

When someone realizes they have been scammed, the obvious question is: Can I get my money back?

A new US initiative aims to improve the chances of intervening before stolen money disappears—and, perhaps more importantly, before victims send more money.

The Threat Disruption Center will connect investigators with participating companies to help pause payments, freeze funds, take down malicious domains, and ban accounts scammers use to approach victims. TRM Labs is providing the investigative technology behind the effort.

TRM Labs is an existing blockchain intelligence company that helps financial institutions, crypto businesses, and government agencies detect and investigate crypto-related financial crime and fraud. It has been selected as the center’s primary private-sector partner.

The Threat Disruption Center sits within the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center, which is co-led by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. It will serve as a shared technology and collaboration resource for a task force that includes more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners.

The reason

The practical aim is to help investigators sort through victim reports, connect related activity, and identify opportunities to intervene. TRM’s CEO told Bloomberg that the company is looking at how artificial intelligence (AI) can help triage reports in near real time and highlight cases where quick action could return funds to victims.

Scammers depend on legitimate services to reach people and move their money: social networks, website hosts, banks, payment providers, and cryptocurrency platforms. Those dependencies also create opportunities to interrupt them.

The center is intended to provide a standing channel through which investigators and participating companies can share intelligence in near real time. Depending on the circumstances, a company could then:

  • Pause a victim’s payment
  • Freeze stolen funds
  • Take down a malicious domain
  • Ban a social media account used to approach victims

The intended beneficiaries are anyone targeted by scams, cybercrime, and sextortion, not just people who own cryptocurrency. For consumers, the most valuable intervention may be the payment they never make.

Cryptocurrency investment scams often unfold over time. A scammer builds trust, introduces an apparently profitable investment opportunity, and encourages the victim to keep adding money. The FBI says some victims identified through its existing Operation Level Up initiative were preparing to sell their homes, liquidate retirement savings, or take out substantial loans. Reaching someone before that next transfer can prevent an already serious loss from becoming much worse.

What it’s not

Tracing money, freezing it, seizing it, and returning it to a victim are different stages. The announcements describe interventions intended to preserve funds while investigations and legal proceedings continue.

It should not be mistaken for a new public-facing recovery service, and it does not guarantee that victims will get their money back. The announced route for reporting a scam remains the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, or IC3.

Do not wait for a new initiative to reach you. The FBI recommends:

  • Stop sending money immediately. Do not pay additional “taxes,” “verification charges,” or withdrawal fees demanded by a suspicious investment platform.
  • Report the scam promptly at ic3.gov. Rapid reporting can support recovery efforts and help investigators connect related complaints.
  • Be wary of anyone offering to recover your money for a fee. Recovery services can themselves be scams.
  • Verify unexpected contact from law enforcement independently. The FBI warns that criminals impersonate agents and legitimate anti-fraud operations. Contact your local FBI field office to verify an approach rather than relying on an email’s appearance.
  • If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you assess it and suggest next steps.

articles.title: Vaccine history and the erosion of public trust
articles.content:
Podcast: Play in new window | Download | Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | iHeartRadio | Podcast Index | RSS

Why are so many Americans questioning vaccines—and why is the conversation so often focused on their skepticism rather than the history behind it? In this episode of The Nurses Report, we examine documented vaccine failures, compulsory vaccination laws, research ethics controversies, and the financial influence of powerful organizations over global health policy.

Our investigation begins in nineteenth-century England, when parents faced fines and even imprisonment for refusing compulsory smallpox vaccination. The massive 1885 Leicester protest reminds us that the conflict between government authority and medical autonomy is hardly new.

We also revisit the history of measles mortality, which declined substantially in England and the United States before routine measles vaccination. Drawing a connection to Florence Nightingale’s work during the Crimean War, we discuss the importance of nutrition, sanitation, safer water, ventilation, and nursing care in changing survival outcomes. Measles infections remained widespread before vaccination, but falling death rates deserve their own place in the historical record.

Then we examine the 1955 Cutter incident, when improperly inactivated polio vaccines caused polio, paralysis, and deaths. We explore the discovery that some polio vaccines produced between 1955 and 1963 were contaminated with simian virus 40 (SV40), and why the question of long-term follow-up matters. Although population studies have not established a cancer link, a 2002 Institute of Medicine review found the epidemiological evidence insufficient to accept or reject causation and identified important exposure-measurement limitations. What does meaningful accountability look like decades after a manufacturing failure?

The episode also investigates the Gates Foundation’s substantial funding of WHO and Gavi and asks who should set international healthcare priorities. We discuss the Gates-funded PATH HPV vaccination demonstration project in India, which a parliamentary committee criticized for serious informed-consent and oversight failures involving young girls. In Kenya, we examine allegations surrounding a tetanus vaccination campaign and the history of experimental hCG-based contraceptive vaccines; the claim that the Kenyan campaign covertly sterilized women was not substantiated.

Other cases include the Dengvaxia controversy in the Philippines, where vaccination increased the risk of severe dengue among certain recipients; vaccine-derived poliovirus associated with live oral vaccines; and documented COVID-19 vaccine safety concerns, including myocarditis and rare clotting disorders. We also examine why observational cancer findings require careful long-term investigation rather than assumptions in either direction.

We also consider how concerns are handled after problems are discovered: who investigates adverse events, how families obtain records, whether research findings are made public, and what meaningful remedies exist for those harmed. History is not only about identifying errors. It is about examining what institutions did once those errors became apparent, how openly they communicated, and whether the people affected had any meaningful say in the response.

Throughout, the central question remains: When institutions make errors, fail to protect informed consent, or wield extraordinary financial and regulatory power, how do they earn back public trust? For patients and parents, transparency, independent oversight, and meaningful medical choice are not optional extras. They are the foundation of ethical healthcare.

The Nurses Report on America Out Loud airs weekdays at 10 AM ET. Listen on iHeartRadio, our world-class media player, or our free apps on Apple, Android, or Alexa. All episodes of The Nurses Report on America Out Loud can be found on podcast networks worldwide, the day after airing on talk radio.

Transcript Summary of this podcast episode ⤵

Public health officials often ask why parents are questioning vaccines. They should spend more time asking what happened to the trust they expect families to place in them. When a parent asks what is known about a vaccine’s risks or why a recommendation changed, that is an opening for care. Treating the question as defiance wastes it.

In Victorian England, parents faced fines for refusing compulsory smallpox vaccination for their infants. It took decades of organized resistance before Parliament created a path for conscientious objection. During COVID-19, employment consequences brought an old question back into everyday life: How voluntary is a medical decision when saying no can cost you your livelihood?

Families also have reason to ask how institutions respond when something goes wrong. In 1955, a manufacturing failure at Cutter Laboratories left infectious poliovirus in some doses of a vaccine meant to protect children. Children were paralyzed, and some died. The disaster led to tighter oversight. Those changes mattered, but they came after families had already paid the price.

Honesty also means telling the whole story of prevention. Florence Nightingale’s work during the Crimean War showed what clean wards, better ventilation, and adequate food could mean for patients. Measles deaths fell substantially before vaccination, while measles itself remained widespread. Vaccination later drove down infections. Families deserve to hear that distinction plainly.

No one should expect medicine to get everything right the first time. We should expect officials to explain what went wrong, what changed, and what they still don’t know. At the bedside, informed consent means giving people enough time and clear information to make a decision they understand. It also means respecting their right to refuse. If public health wants to earn back trust, that is where it should start. And families should keep asking questions, even when the answers are uncomfortable.

I find interesting. We’re constantly hearing about vaccine hesitancy. It’s becoming this enormous concern for public health officials. They want to know why people are questioning vaccines, why parents are asking more questions, and why there’s so much distrust in the healthcare system.

But I have a question. Why is everyone so concerned about the lack of trust, but nobody seems nearly as interested in what caused people to lose that trust in the first place? I mean, seriously. You can’t spend decades making mistakes, covering up failures, dismissing people’s concerns, and sometimes outright violating their rights, and then act surprised when people start asking questions.

That’s not how trust works. And I think this is where we have a real disconnect between the medical establishment and the people it’s supposed to serve. Somewhere along the way, questioning medical authority became almost synonymous with being anti-science. And as a nurse, I find that incredibly troubling.

Because isn’t questioning things part of what we’re supposed to do? We’re supposed to evaluate evidence. We’re supposed to identify problems. We’re supposed to advocate for patients.

And when something doesn’t seem right, we’re supposed to speak up. Yet when patients and parents question recommendations, particularly when it comes to vaccines, they’re often treated like they’re the problem. And I think we have that backwards because history matters. And there’s some chapters in medical history that are downright disturbing.

I’m talking about children who were harmed by the products that were supposed to protect them, families punished for refusing medical procedures, medical research involving vulnerable populations where informed consent was seriously compromised. And we’re not talking about rumors or something somebody posted on social media. We’re talking about events documented in historical records, government investigations, and published research. So when someone tells me that people just need to trust the experts, my response is pretty simple.

Trust is earned, but it’s not something you get to demand because you have a medical degree, a government title, or billions of dollars behind you. And here’s the thing I don’t think most people expect medicine to be perfect. We’re human, we make mistakes, science evolves, and we learn things along the way. But there’s a difference between making a mistake and refusing to take accountability for it.

There’s a difference between genuine genuinely educating someone and pressuring them into compliance. And there’s definitely a difference between informed consent and simply getting someone to do what you’ve already decided that they should do. So that’s what we’re going to get into today. Because the more I look into the history, the more I find myself asking the same question.

If these institutions really want to rebuild public trust, why aren’t they the ones leading the conversation on where they’ve gone wrong? And what’s especially interesting is that the battle between medical authority and individual freedom did not start with COVID-19. It didn’t even start in our lifetime. People were fighting over these very issues more than 170 years ago.

And some of them were actually being thrown into jail over it. So let’s go back to England in the 1800s because I think you’re going to find this history pretty eye-opening. Of course, I am your Thursday host, Ashley Caputo on America Out Loud. And I’m so glad that you’re joining me in this conversation because it’s really, really interesting.

And if you haven’t dove into the history of vaccines, we’re gonna just touch on the surface of it so we can condense this into an hour-long show, but there’s so much more to it. So I’d encourage you to dive into it if you like going down some rabbit holes. So let’s let’s start in England in 1853. The British government passed legislation making smallpox vaccination compulsory for infants, meaning mandated.

Parents who refused could face fines. Then in 1967, they actually strengthened enforcement, and persistent refusal could ultimately lead to imprisonment. Think about that. Parents were facing legal punishment for refusing a medical intervention for their children.

And families began fighting back. Organizations formed to oppose compulsory vaccinations. Parents organized protests, published newspapers, they challenged government authority and demanded the right to make medical decisions for their families. And then in 1885, something extraordinary happened.

In Licaster, England, a massive demonstration against mandated vaccines drew a crowd of over 100,000 people. In the 19th century, with no internet, no social media, yet tens of thousands, tens of thousands of people organized around medical freedom and parental rights. And this wasn’t simply a protest over one vaccine. It was a conflict of over how much authority the government should have over individual medical decisions.

The resistance became so significant that Parliament eventually started to change the law. So in 1898, Britain introduced a contentious objection provision allowing qualifying parents to obtain exemptions. But listen to that wording. A provision allowing qualifying parents to obtain exemptions.

So if you weren’t a qualifying parent and you didn’t get an exemption, you were still forced under their law to get this vaccine without the right of refusal, and you still ran the risk of fines and imprisonment if you refused. So it was a start, but it was it was not much because it actually took decades of organized resistance, fines, prosecutions, and imprisonment before the government formally recognized a path for objection. But there’s another part of history that deserves attention. 19th century vaccination wasn’t administered using the same production and safety standards we have today, right?

Some smallpox vaccination methods involved transferring biological material from one person’s arm to another. There were concerns about contamination and the transmission of other infections. So when parents objected, their concerns weren’t exclusively philosophical. Some were worried about what was actually being introduced to their child’s bodies.

And this raises an important question about medical history. How do governments respond when citizens question the safety of a medical procedure that the government has made mandatory? Do they respond by giving more information? Do they investigate concerns?

Or do they punish people for refusing? In Victorian England, the legal penalties became an enormous source of resentment. And I want you to think about the parallels with more recent history. During COVID, people faced employment consequences and restrictions over vaccination decisions.

So once again, the debate became more about that particular medical product. It became about government authority, medical autonomy, and the consequences of refusal, not just the vaccine itself. When does public health recommendations cross that line into medical coercion? That question was being asked in Victorian England.

And we’re still asking that today. So this is something I think that really gets overlooked as well. And it’s not, it’s not talked about a lot when we talk about like history and infectious diseases. There were enormous improvements in health and survival that occurred before many modern vaccines were even introduced.

During the 19th and 20th centuries, mortality from numerous infectious diseases declined dramatically across England and Wales. And there were some major changes that were taking place in society that contributed to this. Clean water systems expanded, sewage systems improved, housing conditions gradually improved, food availability and nutrition improved, and medical care became more effective. Now, as a nurse, I want to connect this history to one of the most influential figures in nursing, Florence Nightingale.

Okay, because what happened during the Crimean War, I think really illustrates the tremendous impact that sanitation, nutrition, and environmental conditions can have on patient survival. So in 1854, Nightingale was sent to a British military hospital, what’s now Istanbul, Turkey. And British soldiers were dying in alarming numbers, and not because of battlefield injuries. They were dying from infectious diseases.

The hospital conditions were appalling. The wards were overcrowded, there were dirty linens, vermin, inadequate bathing facilities, and poor ventilation. You can actually find Florence Nightingale’s letters that she sent describing the conditions, and it’s pretty atrocious. So the food and the medical supplies, they were insufficient.

And this is disgusting. Damaged drainage and sewage systems contributed to dangerous sanitary conditions. Under the hospital, there was sewage drainage problems that were contaminating the hospital. So imagine being a soldier who is putting your life online fighting in war, and you survived the battlefield with an injury, only to arrive at a hospital where the conditions themselves expose you to further illness and death.

So Nightingale arrives and she recognized exactly what was wrong right away. She organized nursing care, she worked to improve cleanliness, she secured supplies, they had to get more supplies sent in and they had to get improved food. They had to get food sent in, they improved food preparation, and they just emphasized basic hygiene and nutrition. One of the most important developments came because the Sanitary Commission arrived in March 1855 and began addressing the hospital’s environmental problems.

Now, Florence Nightingale had to push and push and push for this to be addressed. And so when they finally showed up and they finally started addressing this, they cleaned and repaired drainage systems. They addressed the sewage problems, they improved ventilation, and they worked to make hospital environment safer. And here’s something that’s particularly striking.

By February 1855, the hospital’s mortality rate had reached approximately 42%, according to historical accounts. Nightingale initially placed considerable emphasis on inadequate nutrition, but the most dramatic improvement in mortality occurred after they started addressing the sewage and the ventilation problems. So it just demonstrates how dangerous hospital environment had become, right? So Nightingale later became the leading advocate for sanitation, fresh air, nutrition, cleanliness, and the importance of environment and recovery.

And then she used those statistics to demonstrate how much suffering and death were associated with preventable conditions. And that’s an important lesson in nursing history. It wasn’t a pharmaceutical that she brought in that saved people’s lives. It was literally cleaning up the environment, providing them clean water and nutritious food, providing them with nursing care, bathing them, better ventilation.

The conditions surrounding a patient can profoundly influence whether a patient survives. And these soldiers needed clean surroundings. They needed all of this, the adequate food. Can you imagine being malnourished and trying to recover from a wound in the battlefield and then developing an infection and still not having the nutrition or the clean water or the clean environment to help you recover?

And then you have poor ventilation with sewage seeping into the hospital. So let’s connect this to measles. Routine measles vaccination did not begin in England and Wales until 1968. Yet mortality of measles had already declined dramatically before that before the vaccines were released.

And the U.S. experienced a similar pattern. So this wasn’t just a fluke, but in the early 20th century, it was reported about approximately 6,000 measles-related deaths annually in the United States. Decades before the measles vaccine was introduced in 1963, the number of deaths related to measles had declined to approximately 450 to 500 a year. So that is more than a 90% decline in annual reported measles deaths.

This is before vaccinations were available. So the measles’ infections remained widespread. So the same amount of people were getting measles, it’s the mortality had decreased significantly. So understanding that distinction, I think, is really essential when we’re talking about the history of measles and the role that vaccine played, because they can say, we eradicated measles and people stopped getting measles and nobody was dying from measles.

But you can’t generalize it. There’s two different scenarios here. The incidence of measles was still high. People were still getting measles, but the mortality of measles reduced by 90% just from environmental and sanitary conditions improving.

So decades before the vaccine was even available, the mortality rate had decreased. People were still getting measles, not as many people were dying. And then when the vaccine came on board, less people were getting measles. So the incidence of measles decreased.

But the mortality rate of dying when you had measles, that decreased. Okay. So you you can’t intertwine the two. And they like to be very general when you talk about measles and how the measles vaccine basically eradicated measles.

I’m talking about the mortality, people dying from measles. So when you think about the likelihood of dying, we’re we’re talking about 6,000 people dying versus like 500, that’s a drastic decrease. Obviously, we don’t want anybody dying from measles, but you have to really look at like why did that happen? What changed so much to reduce that?

And it really comes down to environment and sanitation and nursing care and the improvement in medical, like supportive care, right? And these trends were documented. There was a medical historian who documented these historical trends, and he emphasized the importance of living standards and nutrition in reducing mortality. And I think his work raised important questions, right?

How much of the improvement in population health actually came from medical interventions and how much came from changing the conditions in which people live? And I believe Florence Nightingale, her experience provides a powerful illustration of why those environmental factors deserve attention because sanitation, adequate nutrition, and proper care can change outcomes. But there’s also another part of the measles story that we need to discuss. Let’s talk about the original vaccines themselves.

In 1963, two measles vaccines were licensed in the United States. One was a live attenuated vaccine, the other was a killed virus or inactivated vaccine. But the inactivated vaccine developed a serious problem. Some people who were receiving this vaccine later developed a condition what they call atypical measles.

Atypical measles involved high fever, unusual rashes, pneumonia, and other complications, causing hospitalizations and severe illness, right? So the vaccine itself failed to provide the intended protection for the people that it was being distributed to. And in 1967, the inactivated measles vaccine was withdrawn. The original live vaccine also caused substantial reactions, and that eventually was withdrawn and replaced by a quote unquote safer formula, an attenuated formulation.

Then in 1989, recommendations changed to include a second measles vaccine. So initially there was only one, and then in 1989, they recommended a second measles vaccine dose because there were outbreaks at schools or among school children that had received just the single dose. So say think about that timeline. Vaccines were introduced, problems were identified, products changed, recommendations changed, and the public was expected to adapt to those changes.

This history raises questions about what information was available when the original vaccines were introduced. What did the researchers know about the duration of protection? How were adverse reactions monitored? How quickly were problems recognized, and what information was provided to parents when recommendations changed?

Because when a product is being administered to children, families deserve to understand its history. If parents want to know what happened with the previous vaccines, why should they be treated as though asking those questions are unreasonable? These aren’t like these aren’t imaginary events, these aren’t conspiracy theories. I don’t have a tinfoil hat on.

These are a part of documented medical history. And it gets worse. So let’s move on to one of the most notorious vaccine manufacturing disasters in American history. So the SALK polio vaccine was licensed in April 1955.

Polio was feared because of its potential to cause paralysis and the iron lung. Remember that? You’ve seen like pictures in history of kids put into this iron lung, kids paralyzed, kids dying. So there was tremendous public demand for a vaccine, for some intervention to save these children.

But as vaccination programs expanded, states began incorporating polio vaccination into school entry requirements. There was no universal federal law requiring every American to receive the polio vaccine. However, some states made vaccination a condition of school attendance. So I think this is a very sneaky way to mandate vaccines, right?

Like the government tells you you have a choice, you have medical freedom, you can choose to get this vaccine or not. But then the schools turn around and make them required for entry. So, how what decision do you actually have if your kid has to go to school? It’s mandated.

So just because there’s not a federal mandate in place doesn’t mean that parents feel like they have the freedom of choice. If you’re if your child can’t attend school without receiving a medical intervention, how voluntary is that decision? But the polio story, I think, becomes even more troubling when we look at just what happened shortly after the vaccine was was released, was introduced. So in 1955, batches of polio vaccine, they were, it was manufactured by cutter laboratories, and it contained infectious polio virus.

Now, this it was supposed to be an inactivated vaccine. So the virus was supposed to have been inactivated during the manufacturing. But instead, a manufacturing failure allowed infectious virus to remain in some of those batches. And those batches, they passed safety testing, right?

Safe and effective, safe and effective. But it passed the safety test testing, and then it was administered to children. Children received the vaccine. The cases of polio began appearing, and more than 250 cases were attributed, and this is government numbers, okay?

Historical accounts actually say that it was much higher, but more than 250 polio cases were attributed to the contaminated cutter vaccines. Approximately 200 paralysis cases and 10 deaths were associated. Children developed the disease that they had been vaccinated against, and some of them were left permanently disabled, and others died. Imagine being a parent.

You thought you were protecting your child from polio, only to discover that the product administered to your child contained infectious polio virus. You just gave your kid polio. The Cutter incident, I think, is it did become one of the most serious vaccine manufacturing disasters in American history. And it did lead to manufacturing standards and regulatory oversight, which is great.

But those changes came after children had already suffered. When manufacturers and regulators make catastrophic mistakes, who pays the price? It’s the families, the children. It’s the people who trusted that the product had been properly manufactured and tested.

It’s the people who blindly trust that it’s safe and effective. And why shouldn’t you trust your doctor? Why shouldn’t the doctors trust the scientists who tell you this product is safe and effective? History tells us why.

And that wasn’t the only controversy involving early polio vaccines. There’s more. So we do have to take a break. And when we come back from the break, we’re gonna talk about the contamination of the polio vaccine with SV40.

So stick with us. We’re gonna hear from our sponsors. You are listening to The Nurses Report on America Out Loud, and we’ll be right back. Are you struggling with thinning hair?
