You and I want to test the welcome back to the Nurses Report on America Out Loud. I’m your host, Ashley Caputo, and we have been talking about the dark history of vaccines. So if you missed the first half of the segment, I would I would encourage you to go back and listen to it because we we talk about some really dark events that happened in our history and has just created this distrust with public health over the years. So I wanted to continue talking about the polio vaccine because this is one of the most disturbing chapters in the history of polio vaccines, right?

And I think that the research that followed deserves much closer examination. So dates, right? Between 1955 and 1963, some polio vaccines administered in the United States were contaminated with the Simeon virus 40 or SV40. The contamination originated in monkey kidney cells used during vaccine manufacturing.

Historical estimates suggest that approximately 30% of polio vaccines administered during that period were contaminated, meaning millions of Americans were potentially exposed. And scientists discovered something concerning about this virus because they found out the vaccine’s contaminated with this virus. Now we have to study this virus. Like we have to see what the fallout’s gonna be.

What is this virus gonna do? So the SV40 was capable of producing tumors in laboratory animals and transforming cells in experimental systems. So that immediately raised questions about whether exposure could contribute to cancer in humans. Now think about the scale of what had happened.

Millions of people potentially received a medical product containing a virus that was never supposed to be there. The contamination was discovered around 1960, and investigators began examining its possible consequences. But there’s a question I want to focus on. What happened to the people that received these contaminated vaccines?

Were they followed for the remainder of their lives? Was their cancer diagnoses tracked? Did researchers identify exactly who had received contaminated vaccine lots? And did they compare those people’s health outcomes with individuals who had not been exposed?

Because when you’re dealing with potential cancer risks, the length and the quality of the follow-up matters. Some cancer takes decades to develop. A person exposed as an infant in 1960 might not develop certain cancers until their 50s, 60s, 70s. So a study that only examines the first 20 or 30 years of life may not fully answer the question of lifetime cancer risks.

And here’s where the research becomes particularly interesting. Okay, a 35-year follow-up study. In 2001, researchers published a study examining the mortality of 1,073 individuals who had received SV40 contaminated polio vaccines as newborns between 1961 and 1963. This was an unusual cohort because exposure was documented rather than simply estimated from birth dates.

The researchers used death records to examine long-term mortality. Now, the study did not identify a significant overall increase in cancer deaths, but it did identify something that deserves attention. Two deaths from testicular cancer occurred in the group. The number statistically expected was approximately like 0.05 or yeah, 0.05.

Two observed deaths compared with 0.05 expected. So that difference was statistically significant. And researchers acknowledged that it might have been a chance, a chance finding because multiple comparisons were made, right? So, but they also stated that further investigation of testicular cancer might be warranted, and they emphasized the importance of continuing to monitor the cohort as it reached middle age.

So I want you to think about that. A group of newborns received vaccines known to be contaminated with SV40. Researchers followed their mortality records for decades and found an unusual can’t testicular cancer mortality result. And they specifically recommended continued monitoring.

So what happened? Were those individuals followed into their 60s, into their 70s? Were later cancer diagnoses recorded rather than only deaths? Was the testicular cancer finding investigated and in a larger group with individually documented exposure?

Those are the questions that I want answered because only 1,000 people, a little over a thousand people, were actually followed. And millions of people received this vaccine that was contaminated. The next step should be determining what that finding actually means. Like you have this information and then it just stops.

In 2002, the Institute of Medicine conducted a formal review titled Immunization Safety Reviews SV40 contamination of polio vaccine and cancer. Okay. And the findings are worth examining carefully. The committee reviewed these studies, like laboratory research and evidence concerning the possible association between SV40 contaminated vaccines and cancer.

And the committee concluded that the evidence was inadequate to either accept or reject a causal relationship between SV40 containing polio vaccine and cancer. Now, I want to explain why I read that verbatim, and I want to explain why I think the wording matters. The committee itself identified limitations in the available research. So in many studies, researchers did not know which individuals had actually received contaminated vaccines.

Exposure was often just estimated using the birth years because some batches were contaminated, but not all vaccine was contaminated. And they used periods of time when they thought contaminated products were in circulation. So right there, the research is not very reliable, right? It doesn’t establish like which manufacturer produced the vaccine.

It doesn’t establish whether the particular dose was contaminated, and it doesn’t establish like how much SV40 might have been present. So some of these studies just relied on estimated exposure rather than individually documented exposure. And that is challenging when you’re attempting to investigate long-term health outcomes. Even if you found that there was an increase in cancer risk, they’re going to come back and say, well, there’s flaws in your research.

So when a condition is, uncommon, like this testicular cancer, very large populations and adequate follow-up may be necessary to really detect if there’s a meaningful difference, in people that received the vaccine and didn’t. And remember, they were only looking at like a thousand people. And then there’s another issue. Some individuals in the study had not reached the ages when certain cancers became more common.

So, for example, like mesothelioma may have long latency periods. So the age of the of the follow-up, it matters. The timeline matters. And there’s something else I want to talk about.

A study examining cancer mortality is not necessarily the same as a study examining cancer incidence. Mortality measures who died from cancer and incidence measures who developed cancer. And those are two different outcomes. Some people may develop cancer, receive treatment, and survive.

That person may never appear in a study examining only cancer deaths. So when evaluating whether, the exposure to this SV40 increases cancer risk, I think it matters whether researchers actually measured diagnosis or simply just mortality. And then it also, then you have the problem with the SV40, it’s not even confirmed that they had actual exposure. So there’s just so many flaws in the research.

They really dropped the ball on all of this. So I guess if you want to talk about like what was actually established, the researchers conducted long-term studies, and several did not identify a general increase in cancer risk. But those studies were not all equivalent to following millions individually confirmed with SV 40 exposed people, . So it’s just very unreliable, didn’t really tell us anything, and was probably just a waste of funding the way that they they went about this research.

And they acknowledge, in in the research that there’s there’s limitations. So I just want to ask, like, where’s the comprehensive lifelong follow-up of these individuals with verified exposure? They should have taken the time to find the the lot numbers and the batches that that had contamination and found the people that had received those vaccines. There’s just so many questions left unanswered, which is another reason that people don’t trust public health, people don’t trust the government, and people don’t trust research because the research, a lot of the times, is very unreliable.

And the absence of definitive proof of harm is just not the same as definitive proof that no harm occurred, right? When millions of people were potentially exposed to an unintended virus with tumor-producing properties in experimental systems, the quality of lifelong, long-term surveillance that matters. And this is why I believe like this story deserves more attention. It’s not just about historical manufacturing failure, but it’s about what happens afterwards.

How thoroughly we investigate, how do we continue monitoring? Who decides when enough research has been conducted? And how much of that information is actually communicated to the public. There is no transparency.

Because once a medical product has been administered to millions of people, an investigation shouldn’t just end with simply acknowledging that a mistake occurred. We should want to understand the consequences. And one more thing to mention about the SV40, once it was realized that the these vaccines were contaminated, I’m sure they recalled them, right? They pulled them off the market, they pulled them out of circulation.

No, no, they continued administering the vaccines that they knew were contaminated. That is a problem. Why doesn’t the public trust you? There’s one of your answers right there.

The proof is in the history. So let’s let’s shift our attention to Bill Gates. Most people know Bill Gates, right? Is and if you’ve listened to me, we have talked about Bill Gates before.

And I’m not a fan. So, but if you’re unfamiliar with Bill Gates, he is the co-founder of Microsoft. But through the Gates Foundation, he has become one of the most financially influential private individuals in global healthcare. Co-founder of Microsoft is one of the most financially influential private individuals in global health care.

How does that even I don’t know? His foundation has contributed up to billions, billions of dollars towards vaccine research, infectious disease programs, pharmaceutical development, and international vaccination initiatives. It has provided significant funding to the World Health Organization, Gavi, and the Global Polio Eradication Initiative. I want to ask a fundamental question here.

Why should one unelected billionaire have this much influence over global health care priorities? We’re talking about financial resources large enough to shape research priorities, support particular interventions, and influence which international health initiatives receive funding. That’s a lot of power. Right.

And there’s a there’s a difference between donating money to healthcare and becoming one of the largest financial supporters of institutions that help determine determine international health policy. And like my question, who oversees that influence? Right? Who determines which initiatives receive priority?

And most importantly, who represents communities affected by those decisions? And what happens when a major donor’s funding, when their priorities differ from the needs identified by local healthcare professionals. Because having billions of dollars should not make someone like an elected representative of the people affected by those decisions, right? Like Bill Gates is not an elected official.

We should be allowed to scrutinize his organization. So let’s follow the money. In October 2025, a study published in BMJ Global Health examined the financial relationship between the Gates Foundation and the World Health Organization. The researchers analyzed grants made between 2000 and 2024.

And what I think what they found, I really think deserves more attention than it gets. Like you never hear about this stuff, right? During that period, the Gates Foundation awarded approximately $5.5 billion to the WHO through 640 grants. $5.5 billion, billion with a B, billion dollars.

Now let’s examine where that money went. Let’s follow the money. Approximately $4.5 billion was directed towards infectious disease. That’s nearly 83% of the foundation’s grant funding.

Approximately $3.2 billion went towards polio, and approximately $2.9 billion funded vaccine-related programs and projects. Now, this is where it becomes interesting here. Remember what we discussed earlier about Florence Nightingale: sanitation, clean water, adequate nutrition, safe living conditions. We talked about the role of environmental factors and determining whether someone survives an illness.

According to that same published analysis, approximately $11.8 million of the Gates Foundation’s WHO grants went towards water and sanitation. Compare that with $3.2 billion for polio. $3.2 billion for polio compared with approximately $11.8 million for water and sanitation. These figures concern the foundation’s grants to WHO.

Not everything it is funded like worldwide, right? So, but they do show how this particular funding was allocated. And I just want you to consider that. The researchers also examined how grants were structured.

And here’s another important detail. Grants were earmarked. I didn’t really know what that meant. So I looked it up for us.

It means money is designated for specific purposes. I think I’ve heard it before. I just didn’t really, pay attention to what that meant. But you hear about grants, you can be given what I think they call them what block grants.

Like you’re given, you’re given money, and like let’s say it’s given to a state. And that state can use it however they need. But then you have you have certain grants that are given where the money is already designated for specific purposes. So that’s what we’re talking.

So it’s not unrestricted funding that the WHO can direct wherever it identifies the greatest need, the donor Bill Gates, the donor specifies the purpose of the grant. So when a foundation supplies billions in earmarked funding, like those choices influence where the programs receive resources. And if global health organizations does depend heavily on designated contributions from private donors, like whose priorities are ultimately shaping the agenda? So let’s talk about Gavi, the vaccine alliance.

Gavi was established in 2000 as an international public private partnership supporting vaccination programs, particularly in lower income countries. And partnerships involve they involve governments, international organizations, civil society, and the vaccine industry, of course. And the Gates Foundation helped launch Gavi with an initial commitment of $750 million, three-quarters of a billion dollars, and its financial support continued on. Gavi helps finance vaccine procurement and delivery.

That involves purchasing agreements, contracts, manufacturers, pricing negotiations, and decisions whether products receive financial support. So when international organizations face large-scale purchases of pharmaceutical products, the financial arrangements deserve scrutiny. How much flexibility does it have to direct resources towards other needs? And are local communities involved in making those decisions?

Let’s talk about something a little more disturbing. So between 2009 and 2010, approximately 24,000 girls in India participated in an HPV vaccination demonstration project. And I would put emphasis on the word participated, because that implies that you actively knew what you were doing. Many of the girls, though, came from disadvantaged, like low-income tribal communities, and some were they were only like 10 years old.

And in 2013, the Indian Parliamentary Committee investigated the project and reported serious irregularities. And among the findings were concerns, like serious concerns about informed consent, inadequate documentation, improper authorization, and failures in adverse event monitoring. In some cases, school officials or hostile representatives signed the consent forms for girls that weren’t even related to them. Some of the parents were given consent forms to sign, and they’re not able to read the forms.

And questions were raised whether these families even understood the nature of the project. Seven girls died during the program. Now, I want I want you to think about what we’re discussing. Thousands of girls, many from disadvantaged communities, participating in a project supported by one of the wealthiest foundations in the world.

And serious questions were raised about whether proper informed consent had even been obtained. How can a parent make an informed medical decision when the can the consent process itself is compromised? Lack of wealth or education in a community should never mean its children receive fewer protections. Now let’s talk about Kenya.

In 2014, Catholic bishops and medical organizations in Kenya raised serious allegations about a tetanus vaccine campaign targeting women of reproductive age. This one’s really interesting, y’all. They claim that samples they arranged to have tested contained human chorionic gonadotropin, or easier said, HCG. And as HCG is a hormone involved in maintaining early pregnancy.

These allegations raised fears that women could be receiving something intended to interfere with fertility without them even knowing. And there’s an important historical connection here. This is where it’s really interesting. Researchers had previously investigated experimental contraceptive vaccines designed to stimulate antibodies against HCG.

Some of these experimental formulations used HCG linked to a tetanus-related carrier protein. That research really existed. And the existence of that research became a part of this controversy in Kenya. So Catholic medical leaders publicly challenged the campaign and they called for further investigation.

They described their concerns and laboratory testing they had arranged to test these vaccines. And of course, the WHO, UNICEF, and Kenyan health authorities, they disputed the allegations. The original laboratory claims were contested. They found evidence that there were substances in there to create HCG antibodies in this tetanus vaccine.

Women deserve to understand what they’re receiving and have confidence that the concerns about reproductive health are investigated thorough, thoroughly. You should know the product that you’re getting. They don’t even know the intent of this vaccine initiative. Was it really to give you tetanus vaccines or was it to control population?

In 2019, a malaria vaccine implementation program began in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi. The program involved a vaccine being introduced through national immunization services while researchers evaluated its implementation effects, meaning the public became the study. It was in 2020, I think, that the BMJ published criticism concerning informed consent in the program’s evaluation. So people didn’t really understand that they were a part of research, that that they were the test subjects.

So, of course, critics questioned whether the arrangements met appropriate ethical standards for research involving children. But again, the WHO maintained the vaccine was being administered through routine immunization programs, and the parents, of course, could decline. But this controversy, I think, highlights an important question. When research is conducted alongside routine health care, do families really understand what’s happening?

Do you understand that you are the test subject, that you’re a part of the research study? Do they know which activities involve just ordinary healthcare and which are research? Like, how is informed consent being obtained? So keep asking questions, y’all.

Keep informed, study, look at the research. You have the right to decide what’s going into your body, and you have the right to refuse. We can’t give up on this. We have to keep fighting for medical freedom.

So thank you so much for joining me today. I I love this topic and I would love to talk more about it. But if you guys have topics that you would like to hear me talk about, please reach out to America Out Loud, the Nurses Report. We’d love to hear from you.

So stay safe, y’all. God bless. And until next time, thank you for listening to the Nurses Report. Report.

articles.title: Hackers leak data linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan customers

In this article

  • A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers
  • The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed
  • Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing

Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks.

On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters:

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line.

Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program.

Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole.

What information was exposed?

The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified.

The companies have disclosed the following:

  • JPMorgan Chase: Marketing data held by vendors, potentially including some customer names and email addresses.
  • Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected.
  • Mastercard: A limited number of email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. Mastercard described this as non-payment information.

The n0n leak site lists JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard and claims their data was published after the ransom deadline passed on November 16.

Researchers at Cybernews reported additional details from the leaked datasets:

  • JPMorgan: Roughly 16,000 customer email addresses, some phone numbers, identifiers described as account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses.
  • Visa: A dataset involving more than 6,000 premium customers, with fields including names, email addresses, phone numbers, messaging-app information, and booking details such as dates and addresses.
  • Mastercard: Data posted by n0n includes marketing information related to customers in North America, the Middle East, and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses, according to Reuters.

How to protect your accounts

If you’re concerned your information may be involved, these steps can help protect your accounts and identity:

  • Verify messages independently. Open your bank’s official app, use a website address you already know, or call the number on your card or statement. Do not use a link or phone number supplied by someone claiming to be investigating the breach.
  • Never read out a login or payment-verification code to an unexpected caller. Those codes can be the missing piece that allows a criminal to access your account. Enter them only when completing an action you initiated through the genuine service.
  • Do not transfer money to “protect” it. A caller who tells you to move your savings into a “safe account” is trying to steal them. Hang up and contact your bank independently.
  • Verify any offer of breach support before enrolling. JPMorgan says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.
  • Consider a credit freeze as a separate identity-protection measure.
  • If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard. It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next.

If your data was involved in a breach, read our guide for more advice: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

articles.title: Industry Reactions to Major Outages and AI Patching Debate: Feedback Friday
articles.content:
A series of major technology outages have hit the United States, disrupting email, air travel, banking and government operations.

The incidents included a nearly day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions at other banks, and an outage affecting the NSA’s classified internal network. United Airlines and Apple also experienced disruptions.

Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a link between the incidents. Microsoft traced its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blamed a newly installed router, and the NSA cited routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, however, linked the NSA disruption to patching for a PHP vulnerability found with the help of AI. Sen. Mark Warner said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is pushing organizations to patch many systems at once, putting strain on infrastructure that wasn’t built for that pace of change.

Industry professionals have commented on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role, the need for tested rollback plans, and the fragility of interconnected systems.

And the feedback begins…

Gil Tene, Chief Technology Officer & Co-founder, Azul:

“We have strong reason to believe that AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents. Based on direct experience with customers, we know that urgently deploying large, non-security-only OpenJDK updates does cause stability incidents. These rollouts sometimes fail and have to be reverted, leaving organizations exposed and delaying the remediation of the very vulnerabilities they are meant to address until teams find a workaround they can roll out without compromising stability.

As AI accelerates the discovery of critical flaws, patch cycles are compressing rapidly. In the past four weeks alone, the Java community has had to absorb four update events, including three separate critical vulnerability events and a multitude of high-severity CVEs that couldn’t wait. When a critical Java vulnerability lands, teams must push OpenJDK updates into production within hours, often with less testing than they would normally do and with far more urgency to get the change rolled out before attackers can exploit it. When the fix for a vulnerability is available only as part of a much wider full update that brings along hundreds of unrelated changes, the rollout carries much more risk, because change is risk.

The outage risk doesn’t come from the vulnerabilities themselves. It comes from the volume of change forced by compressed timelines. Hurried, urgent change is risky to begin with. The more change a hurried rollout carries, the greater the risk of instability and widespread incidents. Security-only updates minimize that risk by limiting the change to what is necessary to resolve the vulnerabilities, and nothing more.”

Samuel Hassine, CEO and Co-founder, Filigran:

“I think [faster patching pace driven by AI] plays a part, but I would be careful not to make it the whole story. From what has been made public so far, these outages look less like an AI problem than a change problem: updates and upgrades pushed onto systems that can’t take much change. AI is making that visible, because the list of flaws to fix now grows faster than most companies can safely roll out the fixes.

For years our industry has told companies to patch faster and has measured them on that alone. But a fix that takes the service down is a security failure too, because being available is the first thing a customer expects from you. So the question I would put to every CEO is who owns the choice between leaving a flaw open a few more days and risking the service by closing it tonight. In most companies those are two teams with two different targets, and at this pace it has to be one person who answers for both.”

Ken Barth, CEO, Catalogic Software:

“AI is finding vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes were built to handle. Microsoft fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record, and 1,094 in November. The company has said AI-assisted discovery will put more fixes into each release. Each fix is a change to a live system. With the same staff and maintenance windows, a higher volume leaves less time to test each update, and less testing leaves more room for something to break. Nothing published so far links this pressure to the recent Microsoft 365 outage, but Microsoft’s own explanation shows how easily planned work can take a service down.

Waiting longer is not a safe answer either. Google has reported attackers using AI to reverse-engineer patches and quickly build exploits for the flaws the patches address, so every published fix also tells attackers where to look. That makes being able to undo a change a security control in its own right. Before it reaches production, each update needs a verified restore point for the systems it touches, a tested rollback plan, and a clear owner for the decision to use it.

The same discipline applies after something breaks. Microsoft restored services in stages to keep them stable, which is what careful recovery looks like. Organizations should know before the next incident which services must come back first, what each one depends on, and how long the full sequence takes. A recovery time that has never been tested is only an estimate, and boards should treat it as one.”

Brian Contos, Field CISO, Mitiga:

“Faster patching isn’t the problem by itself. AI is shrinking the time between a vulnerability being disclosed and being exploited, so defenders are under real pressure to ship fixes faster, and every change is a chance to break something. Look at the past week. Officials tied the FAA disruption to a network equipment upgrade, sources told CBS News the NSA outage followed routine patching, and JPMorgan Chase attributed its problems to a software issue. None of those appear to be attacks. What turns a routine change into a national outage is pushing it without being able to see its effects or quickly undo it. Speed is fine if every change is staged, watched for how the system behaves afterward and backed by a rollback someone has tested.

The other lesson is how far a single failure travels. One router change at the FAA destabilized 17 of its 22 en route centers, and Chase said its issue may have slowed transactions at other banks. Redundancy alone doesn’t protect against a healthy component that’s misbehaving, because everything around it trusts it. Segmentation, independent failure domains and a rehearsed process for isolating a bad component quickly are what keep one problem from becoming everyone’s problem.

The preparation for failures and cyberattacks is largely the same. An adversary can deliberately create these same disruptions, coordinate them across multiple locations and interfere with recovery. If a system can’t survive an accident, it won’t survive an adversary.”

Benny Czarny, CEO and Founder, OPSWAT:

“Faster patching can actually contribute to outages when testing and recovery cannot keep up. AI is increasing the pressure to fix vulnerabilities quickly, but you can’t attribute anything to AI without evidence from the investigation.

Failures this week have resulted from cloning systems and their weaknesses along with them. When a primary system and its backup run the same software, receive the same update, and depend on the same network, then they really aren’t that independent.

From a cybersecurity standpoint, critical infrastructure needs the same design mindset as an airplane cockpit, where primary and secondary systems use different hardware and software to reduce the chance that one defect disables every way of performing a critical function.”

Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor, Huntress:

“Right now, there is no definitive link between these outages, and we should be careful about rushing to conclusions that AI or cyberattacks are responsible without having all the facts. What we do know is that there is a significant AI race going on between defenders and threat actors. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders are under increasing pressure to engineer, test and push patches quickly to stay one step ahead. When companies are focused on speed of development, mistakes can happen. In the age of rapid patching, testing and verifying updates is arguably more important than ever.

My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned.

When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.”

Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security:

“This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to the DCA airline crash last year in a sense. After that incident, every near miss got national attention rather than being the usual footnote.

We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.

Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”

Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:

“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously.

AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.

Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”

Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:

“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.

So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”

Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:

“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely.

I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”

Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:

“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage.

A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”

Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 

“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.

Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.

Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”

Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:

“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.

System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.

Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

articles.title: SBC Medical Group Data Breach Impacts Over 2 Million
articles.content:
California-based SBC Medical Group Holdings Incorporated (NASDAQ: SBC) has disclosed a data breach impacting over 2 million individuals in Japan.

The medical services organization provides consulting, management, and operational support to medical corporations and clinics.

Hackers accessed an online platform SBC Medical Group manages and compromised databases containing customer information associated with certain clinics in Japan, the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

SBC Medical Group continues to investigate the attack but has confirmed that personal and medical information was likely compromised.

The hackers stole the basic information of 1,624,000 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, patient card numbers, member IDs, and survey responses.

They also compromised the reservation-request information of 255,416 people, as well as the content entered in web inquiry forms by 217,769 individuals.

According to the filing, 4,513 people also had their treatment descriptions and stored image file names stolen, while 15,007 had the basic information, treatment names, and review text exfiltrated. For 14 individuals, credit card information was also compromised.

“The Company has confirmed that all of these credit cards were in a state in which additional payments could not be processed, such as having expired,” SBC Medical Group said.

Additionally, the hackers stole customer passwords, along with 20,000 records containing employee names, IDs, and passwords.

“For 459 employees, information provided at the time of employment, including bank account and pension-related information, withholding tax certificates and dependent exemption declarations, was also affected,” the company said.

In a separate incident involving the third-party reservation service Tribeau, hackers accessed administrator accounts and accessed the information of approximately 19,000 individuals.

For 12,641 of them, the threat actors compromised Kana names, phone numbers, age, and requested treatments. For three people, the hackers also accessed message contents, dates of birth, and gender, and for 6,804 they compromised reservation information and treatment details.

“The operator confirmed that the obtained information was not linked to case or review information, including photographs, on Tribeau. Email addresses, residential addresses, credit card information, passwords, and electronic medical records were not included in that platform incident. The company and the provider continue to investigate the access and its cause,” the company said.

SBC Medical Group said both incidents have been remediated. It isolated the affected server and evicted the hackers, and rotated the passwords for all the clinics to which it provides management services on Tribeau.

“The company is continuing to assess the potential impact of the incidents on its business, financial condition and results of operations,” SBC Medical Group said.

articles.title: European Commission Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattack Disrupted Services
articles.content:
The European Commission has confirmed falling victim to an AI-assisted cyberattack that disrupted several of its services.

Hackers hit the European Union’s main executive body in late October, and the attack has been largely contained. The investigation into the incident continues, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said during a press conference.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings, as they come,” Regnier said.

The attack was detected on October 22 and was confirmed on October 26. The investigation has found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission’s staff, Regnier added.

According to Politico, the hackers potentially compromised large amounts of data and caused disruptions that lasted over 10 days. Impacted services included the Commission’s HR platform Sysper, medical reimbursement system MyPMO, and translation systems.

While Regnier has confirmed that the hackers used an AI tool during the attack, he did not attribute the incident to a known group and said he was not aware of the Commission receiving a ransom demand related to the attack.

Regnier has not named the AI tool used in the attack, but the disclosure came roughly two weeks after the European Union’s cybersecurity arm CERT-EU warned of threat actors using the AI-powered penetration-testing framework Artex to target its constituency.

“We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” CERT-EU said.

Artex is one of the AI frameworks that threat actors have been increasingly leveraging in attacks, and has been used to hack Barracuda, Railway, ConnectWise customers, and other organizations.

articles.title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
articles.content:
Cryptographers are debating the long-term outlook for public-key cryptography now that AI is proving that hard analytical problems are no longer solvable by humans alone.

Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

“I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added.

These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems.

Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility.

The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail. Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis, told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards.

“We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.”

The math at stake

Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics:

  • Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers)
  • Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc.

“What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO.

Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science.

“The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.”

2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece

Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance.

“A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained.

AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978).

“The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added.

Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.”

Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen.

The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis.

Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’

Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis.

Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded.

Q-Day and LLMs

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography.

“We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.”

Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use.

“We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”
